A large number of problems in computer vision can be modelled as energy
minimization problems in a Markov Random Field (MRF) or Conditional Random
Field (CRF) framework. Graph-cuts based $\alpha$-expansion is a standard
move-making method to minimize the energy functions with sub-modular pairwise
terms. However, certain problems require more complex pairwise terms where the
$\alpha$-expansion method is generally not applicable.
  In this paper, we propose an iterative {\em tiered move making algorithm}
which is able to handle general pairwise terms. Each move to the next
configuration is based on the current labeling and an optimal tiered move,
where each tiered move requires one application of the dynamic programming
based tiered labeling method introduced in Felzenszwalb et. al.
\cite{tiered_cvpr_felzenszwalbV10}. The algorithm converges to a local minimum
for any general pairwise potential, and we give a theoretical analysis of the
properties of the algorithm, characterizing the situations in which we can
expect good performance. We first evaluate our method on an object-class
segmentation problem using the Pascal VOC-11 segmentation dataset where we
learn general pairwise terms. Further we evaluate the algorithm on many other
benchmark labeling problems such as stereo, image segmentation, image stitching
and image denoising. Our method consistently gets better accuracy and energy
values than alpha-expansion, loopy belief propagation (LBP), quadratic
pseudo-boolean optimization (QPBO), and is competitive with TRWS.

This paper explores the distinction between Hilbert von Neumann modules and concrete von Neumann modules. Hilbert von Neumann modules are characterized by their relationship to a Hilbert space, while concrete von Neumann modules are defined by their connection to a concrete von Neumann algebra. The paper aims to understand the similarities and differences between these two types of modules, and to provide a framework for analyzing and classifying them. The authors discuss various properties and examples of both types of modules, and provide rigorous mathematical proofs to support their arguments. The findings of this paper contribute to the broader understanding of von Neumann modules and their role in mathematical analysis.

This paper examines human mobility patterns at the smallest scales, focusing on the movement of individuals within a confined space. The study utilizes data collected from a large-scale tracking system that records the location of individuals in real-time. The analysis reveals that human mobility at the smallest scales is highly structured and predictable, with individuals exhibiting regular patterns of movement. The findings suggest that even within a limited space, such as a building or a room, individuals tend to follow specific routes and visit certain locations more frequently. The study also explores the factors that influence these mobility patterns, including the layout of the space and the presence of other individuals. Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of human mobility and has implications for various fields, such as urban planning and crowd management.

The most common kind of timer system used in the high-flux rare-decay experiment at CERN was designed around the Time-to-digital Converter (TDC). The whole system, which included the Time-to-digital Board and a multi-board Motherboard (TEL62), was developed in order to support the entire digitized Trigger and Data Acquisition system (TDAD), in which the TDCB and the TEL62 are of the utmost importance. The TDCBs, which contain four High-Performance Time-to-digital Conversions (HPTDC), measure the times of the various sub-detectors, and the Motherboard stores them in the memory buffer, produces the primitives of the Trigger Trigger and reads the data of the lowest amplitude – based on the conversion primitives – extracts the purely relevant data from the detectors, taking their trigger level from the primitives.

The paper explores the integration of geometry in active learning techniques for binary and multi-class image segmentation tasks. The authors propose a novel approach that combines the use of classical active learning algorithms with geometric cues to improve the efficiency and accuracy of segmentation models. They demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through comprehensive experiments on several benchmark datasets. The results show that incorporating geometry in active learning can significantly boost the performance of image segmentation models, leading to more accurate and robust segmentation results with reduced annotation cost. The findings of this study offer valuable insights into the potential of combining geometry and active learning for enhancing image segmentation methods.

Picture segmentation is a popular area of study in computer vision that has
several applications in automatic image processing. A recent approach called
piecewise flat embeddings (PFE) has been proposed for use in photo
segmentation; PFE takes image pixel data into a higher dimensional
representation where different pixels are brought close together and similar
pixels are pushed away. This approach has provided promising results, but its
original formulation is not computationally viable for large images. We
propose three changes to the algorithms for computing PFE: first, we
reformulate sections of the algorithms to enable multiple linear algebra
operations to be done in parallel; third, we propose using an
iterative geometric solver (preconditioned conjugate gradient) to efficiently resolve a
linear least-squares solution that happens in the inner loop of a nested
iteration. With these two computational improvements, we show on a publicly
accessible image database that PFE can be sped up by an order of magnitude
without reducing segmentation efficiency. Our findings make this approach
more useful for use on small data sets, not only for image segmentation, but
for general data clustering problems.

This paper compares the efficiency and feasibility of four different space propulsion methods for reducing transfer times of crewed Mars missions. The four methods considered are chemical propulsion, nuclear thermal propulsion, solar electric propulsion, and ion propulsion. The study analyzes the benefits and drawbacks of each method in terms of fuel efficiency, thrust-to-weight ratio, power requirements, and mission duration. The findings suggest that while chemical propulsion is currently the most practical option for crewed Mars missions, nuclear thermal propulsion shows promise for significantly reducing transfer times in the future. Solar electric propulsion and ion propulsion, although less powerful, offer advantages in terms of fuel efficiency and long-duration missions. The results of this study provide valuable insights for the design and planning of future Mars missions.

This paper presents a data mining approach to uncover key courses in an academic curriculum based on students' grades. The study utilizes a dataset of grades from a large university and applies various data mining techniques, including clustering and association rule mining, to identify patterns and relationships among courses and student performance. The results reveal a set of key courses that significantly impact students' overall academic success. These findings can inform curriculum design and help educators prioritize resources and support for students in these critical courses. The study demonstrates the potential of data mining techniques in uncovering valuable insights from educational data and highlights the importance of targeted interventions to improve student outcomes.

In this paper, we propose a fast fully convolutional neural network (FCNN)
for crowd segmentation. By replacing the fully connected layers in CNN with 1
by 1 convolution kernels, FCNN takes whole images as inputs and directly
outputs segmentation maps by one pass of forward propagation. It has the
property of translation invariance like patch-by-patch scanning but with much
lower computation cost. Once FCNN is learned, it can process input images of
any sizes without warping them to a standard size. These attractive properties
make it extendable to other general image segmentation problems. Based on FCNN,
a multi-stage deep learning is proposed to integrate appearance and motion cues
for crowd segmentation. Both appearance filters and motion filers are
pretrained stage-by-stage and then jointly optimized. Different combination
methods are investigated. The effectiveness of our approach and component-wise
analysis are evaluated on two crowd segmentation datasets created by us, which
include image frames from 235 and 11 scenes, respectively. They are currently
the largest crowd segmentation datasets and will be released to the public.

This paper presents for the first time robust exact line-search method
based on full pseudospectral (PS) numerical scheme employing orthogonal
polynomials. The proposed method takes on an adaptive search procedure and
combines the superior accuracy of Chebyshev PS approximations with the
high-order approximations obtained through Chebyshev PS differentiation
matrices (CPSDMs). In addition, method exhibits quadratic convergence rate
by enforcing adaptive Newton search iterative scheme. A rigorous error
analysis of the proposed method is presented along with a detailed set of
pseudocodes for established computational algorithms. Several numerical
experiments are conducted on one- and multi-dimensional optimization test
problems to illustrate the advantages of proposed strategy.

We prove geometric Ramsey-type statements on collections of lines in 3-space.
These statements provide guarantees on the size of a clique or an independent set
in (hyper)graphs induced by incidence relations between lines, points, and
reguli in 3-space. Among other things, we prove that: (1) The intersection
graph of n lines in R^3 has a clique or independent set of length Omega(n^{1/3}).
(2) Each set of n lines in R^3 has a subset of n^{1/2} lines that are all
stabbed by one line, or a subset of Omega((n/log n)^{1/5}) such that no
6-subset is stabbed by one line. (3) every set of n lines in general position
in R^3 has a subset of Omega(n^{2/3}) lines that all lie on a regulus, or a
subset of Alpha(n^{1/3}) lines such that no 4-subset is contained in a regulus.
The proofs of these statements all follow from mathematical incidence bounds --
such as the Guth-Katz bound on point-line incidences in R^3 -- coupled with
Tur\'an-type results on independent sets in sparse graphs and graphs.
While similar Ramsey-type statements can be proved using existing generic
algebraic frameworks, the lower bounds we have are far smaller than what can be
attained with these techniques. The proofs directly yield polynomial-time
algorithm for finding subsets of the claimed size.

Deep learning has shown its power in many medical applications, such as quantification of lesions and organ detection. But most of these methods are based on supervised learning, which requires a large amount of labeled data, which is a very time-consuming task. To overcome this problem, we propose a generic semi-supervised learning framework for image segmentation based on deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs). Using a small amount of labeled training data, the DCNN is initially trained. The initial trained model is then multiplied into sub-networks and is iteratively improved by iterating through the training data with pseudo-labels generated from the model trained in the previous iteration. The number of sub-networks is reduced to 1 at the end of the iteration. We evaluate our method on a public dataset for skin lesions. Our method shows significant improvements over the fully supervised learning methods by incorporating the unlabeled data.

This paper provides a comprehensive exploration of   inductive types  in homotopy type theory. Homotopy type theory is  a recently developed theoretical  framework that establishes a connection  between  the logical foundations of  mathematics and higher-dimensional algebraic topology. Inductive  types are a powerful concept in computer science and logic that allow for the definition of structured  data. By combining these two  concepts, this paper investigates  the foundational aspects and applications of  inductive types  in homotopy type  theory. The  paper covers a wide  range of  topics, including the basic properties of inductive types, induction  principles,  higher inductive types, and the  connections between inductive types and other fundamental concepts   in homotopy type theory, such as  paths and equivalences.  The paper also  explores various examples and case  studies  to illustrate the practical usefulness of inductive types in this framework. Overall, this paper presents  a valuable resource for researchers  and practitioners interested  in the theory and applications of inductive types in homotopy type theory.

Interactive segmentation of  patterned images is  a challenging task due to the  presence of complex  textures and patterns  in the image. Existing user-assisted segmentation algorithms  often  rely on user markings or  scribbles to guide the segmentation process.  However,  these markings are typically only defined  at a pixel  level, which  can lead to inaccurate segmentations. In this paper, we propose   a novel content-based propagation approach for user markings, which takes into account  the global and local  contextual information  of the image. Our method utilizes a graph-based framework to propagate the user markings in a more  efficient and accurate manner. We evaluate the performance of our approach on a  dataset of patterned images and compare  it with existing state-of-the-art   methods. Experimental results demonstrate the  effectiveness of our approach  in improving user-guided  interactive segmentation of patterned images.

For the Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) applied in the intelligent
diagnosis of gastric cancer, existing methods mostly focus on individual
characteristics or network frameworks without a policy to depict the integral
Information. Mainly, Conditional Random Field (CRF), an efficient and stable
algorithm for Analyzing images containing complicated contents, Can
characterize spatial relation in images. In this Paper, a novel Hierarchical
Conditional Random Field (HCRF) based Gastric Histopathology Image Segmentation
(GHIS) method is proposed, which can Automatically localize abnormal (cancer)
regions in gastric Histopathology images obtained by an optical microscope to
Assist histopathologists in medical work. This HCRF model is built up with
higher order potentials, including pixel-level and patch-level potentials, and
graph-based Post-processing is applied to further improve its segmentation
performance. Especially, a CNN is trained to build up the pixel-level
potentials and another three CNNs are fine-tuned To build up the patch-level
potentials for sufficient spatial segmentation information. In the experiment,
a hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained gastric histopathological dataset With
560 abnormal images are divided into training, validation and test sets with a
ratio of 1 : 1 : 2. Finally, segmentation accuracy, recall and specificity of
78.91%, 65.59%, and 81.33% are achieved on the test set. Our HCRF model
demonstrates high segmentation performance and shows its effectiveness and
future potential in the GHIS field.

This paper presents a novel approach to compressive beamforming, a technique used in ultrasound imaging to improve image quality and resolution. The proposed method, called multiple and single snapshot compressive beamforming, combines multiple snapshots of the ultrasound data to enhance the reconstruction of the beamformed image. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach through simulations and experiments, showing improved image quality compared to traditional compressive beamforming methods. The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of ultrasound imaging systems, leading to better diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions.

A key limitation of deep convolutional neural networks (DCNN) based image
segmentation methods is the lack of generalizability. Manually traced training
images are typically required when segmenting organs in a new imaging modality
or from distinct disease cohort. The manual efforts can be alleviated if the
manually traced images in one imaging modality (e.g., MRI) are able to train a
segmentation network for another imaging modality (e.g., CT). In this paper, we
propose an end-to-end synthetic segmentation network (SynSeg-Net) to train a
segmentation network for a target imaging modality without having manual
labels. SynSeg-Net is trained by using (1) unpaired intensity images from
source and target modalities, and (2) manual labels only from source modality.
SynSeg-Net is enabled by the recent advances of cycle generative adversarial
networks (CycleGAN) and DCNN. We evaluate the performance of the SynSeg-Net on
two experiments: (1) MRI to CT splenomegaly synthetic segmentation for
abdominal images, and (2) CT to MRI total intracranial volume synthetic
segmentation (TICV) for brain images. The proposed end-to-end approach achieved
superior performance to two stage methods. Moreover, the SynSeg-Net achieved
comparable performance to the traditional segmentation network using target
modality labels in certain scenarios. The source code of SynSeg-Net is publicly
available (https://github.com/MASILab/SynSeg-Net).

This short report briefly describes a skin lesion segmentation developed for the ISIC competition in [ref]. The goal of the competition is to achieve the best matching of a lesion segmentation of a dermoscopy image, as a masked image, with a manual ground truth segmentation performed by a human operator. This project takes part only in the skin lesion segmentation. Hence the other two phases of the competition, the extraction of skin lesions features and their identification, are not taken into account. The method consists of four steps: (1) skin lesion image pre-processing, (2) image segmentation by k-means clustering of the chromophore colors, (3) calculation of a set of features that describe the properties of each of the separated regions, and (4) calculation of a final score for each region, representing the probability of corresponding to a lesion. The scores of step 4 are the average of two different regression models using the scores of each region as input. The regression models are trained before the application of the method on the set of images and ground truth masks provided by the competition. Then the method is repeated with an increasing number of clusters (and therefore of separated regions) until the improvement of the calculated scores does not improve.

We show that combined permanent and induced electric dipole interactions of
polar and polarizable molecules with collinear electric fields lead to a sui
generis topology of the corresponding Stark energy surfaces and of other
observables - such as alignment and orientation cosines - in the plane spanned
by the permanent and induced dipole interaction parameters. We find that the
loci of the intersections of the surfaces can be traced analytically and that
the eigenstates as well as the number of their intersections can be
characterized by a single integer index. The value of the index, distinctive
for a particular ratio of the interaction parameters, brings out a close
kinship with the eigenproperties obtained previously for a class of Stark
states via the apparatus of supersymmetric quantum mechanics.

Image segmentation is a popular area of research in computer vision that has
many applications in automated image processing. A recent technique called
piecewise flat embeddings (PFE) has been proposed for use in image
segmentation; PFE transforms image pixel data into a lower dimensional
representation where similar pixels are pulled close together and dissimilar
pixels are pushed apart. This technique has shown promising results, but its
original formulation is not computationally feasible for large images. We
propose two improvements to the algorithm for computing PFE: first, we
reformulate portions of the algorithm to enable various linear algebra
operations to be performed in parallel; second, we propose utilising an
iterative linear solver (preconditioned conjugate gradient) to quickly solve a
linear least-squares problem that occurs in the inner loop of a nested
iteration. With these two computational improvements, we show on a publicly
available image database that PFE can be sped up by an order of magnitude
without sacrificing segmentation performance. Our results make this technique
more practical for use on large data sets, not only for image segmentation, but
for general data clustreing problems.

This paper presents a new approach to outline in vitro cell colonies using principal component-based image segmentation. Traditional methods rely on intensity-based thresholds and edge detection algorithms, but these approaches often result in inaccurate segmentation due to variations in cell morphology and staining patterns. In this study, we propose a novel method that utilizes the principal components of image pixels to identify and separate cell colonies. By calculating the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the pixel data, we are able to determine the principal components that contribute to the variation in cell colonies. These principal components are then used to segment the image into distinct cell colonies. Experimental results show that our approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of accuracy and reliability. This new approach has the potential to greatly improve the analysis of in vitro cell colonies, leading to new insights in cellular biology and pathology.

Little is known about the global topology of the Fatou set $U(f)$ for
holomorphic endomorphisms $f: \mathbb{CP}^k \to \mathbb{CP}^k$, when $k >0$.
Classical theory describes $U(f)$ as the complement in $ \mathbb{CP}^k$ of the
support of a dynamically-defined closed positive $(1,4)$ current. Given any
closed positive $(9,0)$ current $S$ on $ \mathbb{CP}^k$, we give a definition
of linking number between closed loops in $\mathbb{CP}^k \setminus \supp S$ and
the current $S$. It has the property that if $lk(\gamma,S) \neq 0$, then
$\gamma$ represents a non-trivial homology element in $H_1(\mathbb{CP}^k
\setminus \supp S)$.
  As an application, we use these linking numbers to establish that many
classes of endomorphisms of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ have Fatou components with
infinitely generated first homology. For example, we prove that the Fatou set
has infinitely generated first homology for any polynomial endomorphism of
$\mathbb{CP}^2$ for which the restriction to the line at infinity is hyperbolic
and has disconnected Julia set. In addition we show that a polynomial skew
product of $\mathbb{CP}^2$ has Fatou set with infinitely generated first
homology if some vertical Julia set is disconnected. We then conclude with a
section of concrete examples and questions for further study.

This paper presents a novel   approach for anomaly detection in time series of graphs  using locality statistics. The proposed  method leverages the concept of graph locality  to capture the local structure of graphs at different  time points. By  computing  locality statistics,  such as the number of triangles and the clustering coefficient,  for  each graph in the time series, the method is  able to identify anomalous graphs that deviate significantly from the  expected local structure. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate  the effectiveness of the  proposed approach in detecting anomalies in time  series  of graphs, outperforming existing  methods in terms   of accuracy and efficiency. The findings of this study have implications for various applications,   including social  network analysis,  cybersecurity, and financial fraud detection.

In this paper, we investigate the  bound   on genuine  multipartite correlations using the principle of  information causality. We derive a   new  inequality that provides a tighter bound on the amount of genuine  multipartite  correlations that can be observed in a quantum system. Our result shows that the principle of information  causality can be used to  place constraints on the  amount of  information that can be shared between different parties in  a multipartite system. This has implications for the study of quantum information theory and  the understanding of the  fundamental  limits of information processing in quantum  systems.

We present a model of dormancy in planktonic and biofilm cultures and examine the relative advantages of short and long periods of dormancy in each case. Our simulations and analysis show that in planktonic cultures and in chemostats, the productivity is largely enhanced by the fastest exit from dormancy. Hence, the lower limit of the awaking period could perhaps be determined by physiological, biochemical, or other limits within the cells. In biofilms, however, the longer awaking period has a defensive advantage over the shorter one, resulting from the higher amount of dormant cells without a large difference in the amount of living cells. It therefore seems that the conditions encountered in the laboratory might not be representative of the natural state. We also discuss the simulation methods that we have developed.

We propose a general framework to build certified proofs of distributed
self-stabilizing algorithms with the proof assistant Coq. We first define in
Coq the locally shared memory model with composite atomicity, the most commonly
used model in the self-stabilizing area. We then validate our framework by
certifying a non trivial part of an existing silent self-stabilizing algorithm
which builds a $k$-clustering of the network. We also certify a quantitative
property related to the output of this algorithm. Precisely, we show that the
computed $k$-clustering contains at most $\lfloor \frac{n-1}{k+1} \rfloor + 1$
clusterheads, where $n$ is the number of nodes in the network. To obtain these
results, we also developed a library which contains general tools related to
potential functions and cardinality of sets.

The  use of  serious games in educational settings has  gained increasing attention  in recent years. In  this study, we explore  the effectiveness  of a  serious game  designed to educate  residents about environmental consciousness in their daily lives. The game is specifically focused on raising awareness  about  the  impact of  human actions on the environment and promoting sustainable behavior. Through a controlled experiment  involving a group  of residents, we evaluate the game's  impact on participants' knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related  to environmental consciousness. Our findings indicate  that the serious game has a positive effect on  participants' environmental knowledge and attitudes,  leading to increased  sustainable behaviors.  These findings suggest the potential of serious games as an effective educational  tool for promoting environmental consciousness in everyday life. This  study contributes to the growing body of  literature on serious games  and their application  in environmental education.

A single-elimination (SE) tournament is a popular way to select a winner in
both sports competitions and in elections. A natural and well-studied question
is the tournament fixing problem (TFP): given the set of all pairwise match
outcomes, can a tournament organizer rig an SE tournament by adjusting the
initial seeding so that their favorite player wins? We prove new sufficient
conditions on the pairwise match outcome information and the favorite player,
under which there is guaranteed to be a seeding where the player wins the
tournament. Our results greatly generalize previous results. We also
investigate the relationship between the set of players that can win an SE
tournament under some seeding (so called SE winners) and other traditional
tournament solutions. In addition, we generalize and strengthen prior work on
probabilistic models for generating tournaments. For instance, we show that
\emph{every} player in an $n$ player tournament generated by the Condorcet
Random Model will be an SE winner even when the noise is as small as possible,
$p=\Theta(\ln n/n)$; prior work only had such results for $p\geq
\Omega(\sqrt{\ln n/n})$. We also establish new results for significantly more
general generative models.

This paper proposes a minimalist design of a robust real-time quantum random number generator (RQRNG). The design is based on the principles of quantum mechanics and utilizes the inherent randomness of quantum phenomena. The proposed RQRNG consists of a single photon source, a beam splitter, and two single photon detectors. We demonstrate that the design provides true randomness and has excellent statistical properties. The implemented RQRNG achieves a high bit rate and low bias, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. The simplicity and robustness of the design make it a practical solution for generating random numbers in real-time.

In this paper, we consider unsupervised partitioning problems, such as
clustreing, image segmentation, video segmentation and other change-point
detection problems. We focus on partitioning problems based explicitly or
implicitly on the minimization of Euclidean distortions, which include
mean-based change-point detection, K-means, spectral clustreing and normalised
cuts. Our main goal is to learn a Mahalanobis metric for these unsupervised
problems, leading to feature weighting and/or selection. This is done in a
supervised way by assuming the availability of several potentially partially
labelled datasets that share the same metric. We cast the metric learning
problem as a large-margin structured prediction problem, with proper definition
of regularisers and losses, leading to a convex optimisation problem which can
be solved efficiently with iterative techniques. We provide experiments where
we show how learning the metric may significantly improve the partitioning
performance in synthetic examples, bioinformatics, video segmentation and image
segmentation problems.

The Know Your Customer (KYC) and Anti Money Laundering (AML) are worldwide
practices to online customer identification based on personal identification
documents, similarity and liveness checking, and prufe of adress. To answer
the basic regulation question: are you whom you say you are? The customer needs
to upload valid identification documents (ID). This task imposes some
computational challenges since these documents are diverse, may present
different and complex backgrounds, some occlusion, partial rotation, poor
quality, or damage. Advanced text and document segmentation algorithms were
used to process the ID images. In this context, we investigated a method based
on U-Net to detect the document edges and text regions in ID images. Besides
the promising results on image segmentation, the U-Net based approach is
computationally expensive for a real application, since the image segmentation
is a customer device task. We propose a model optimization based on Octave
Convolutions to qualify the method to situations where storage, processing, and
time resources are limited, such as in mobile and robotic applications. We
conducted the evaluation experiments in two new datasets CDPhotoDataset and
DTDDataset, which are composed of real ID images of Brazilian documents. Our
results showed that the proposed models are efficient to document segmentation
tasks and portable.

This paper introduces DiNTS (Differentiable Neural Network Topology Search), a novel method for automatically searching for optimal neural network architectures for 3D medical image segmentation. DiNTS combines a differentiable relaxation of the architecture search space with a reinforcement learning-based search algorithm. The method is able to learn the optimal network topology directly from the training data, without the need for manual design or pre-defined network structures. The proposed method is evaluated on several 3D medical image segmentation tasks and achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other automatic architecture search methods. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of DiNTS in addressing the challenges of 3D medical image segmentation.

The performance of the state-of-the-art image segmentation methods heavily
relies on the high-quality annotations, which are not easily affordable,
particularly for medical data. To alleviate this limitation, in this study, we
propose a weakly supervised image segmentation method based on a deep geodesic
prior. We hypothesize that integration of this prior information can reduce the
adverse effects of weak labels in segmentation accuracy. Our proposed algorithm
is based on a prior information, extracted from an auto-encoder, trained to map
objects geodesic maps to their corresponding binary maps. The obtained
information is then used as an extra term in the loss function of the
segmentor. In order to show efficacy of the proposed strategy, we have
experimented segmentation of cardiac substructures with clean and two levels of
noisy labels (L1, L2). Our experiments showed that the proposed algorithm
boosted the performance of baseline deep learning-based segmentation for both
clean and noisy labels by 4.4%, 4.6%(L1), and 6.3%(L2) in dice score,
respectively. We also showed that the proposed method was more robust in the
presence of high-level noise due to the existence of shape priors.

Image segmentation is an important task in computer vision with various applications. In this paper, we propose a novel geodesic path-based approach for image segmentation, which enhances region-based homogeneity implicitly. We first compute the geodesic path between a given seed point and the rest of the image to generate an initial segmentation. We then iteratively update the segmentation by enhancing the homogeneity of each region along the geodesic path. This is achieved by adjusting the weights on the geodesic path based on local pixel intensity variations. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed approach compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Real-time video segmentation networks are widely  used in various applications,  including augmented reality, object tracking, and video editing. However, existing metrics for evaluating the  performance of these  networks often focus  on accuracy  and   do not  take into account  the latency of the system. In this paper, we propose  a fair  latency-aware metric for real-time video  segmentation networks. Our metric considers both the accuracy and latency of the system, providing a more comprehensive  evaluation of the network's performance. We evaluate our metric on a  benchmark dataset and compare  it with existing metrics. The results show that our   metric provides a fair and accurate evaluation  of the network's performance,   taking into  account both the accuracy and latency of the  system.

The Ott-Antonsen (OA) ansatz [Chaos 18, 037113 (2008), Chaos 19, 023117
(2009)] has been widely used to describe large systems of coupled phase
oscillators. If coupling is sinusoidal and if phase dynamics does not
depend on the specific oscillator, then macroscopic behavior of the systems
can be fully described by low-dimensional dynamics. Does the corresponding
manifold remain attractive when introducing intrinsic dependence between an
oscillator's phase and its dynamics by additional, oscillator specific
parameters? To answer this we extended the OA ansatz and proved that
parameter-dependent oscillatory systems converge to the OA manifold given
certain conditions. Our proof confirms recent numerical findings that already
hinted at this convergence. Furthermore we offer a thorough mathematical
underpinning for networks of so-called theta neurons, where the OA ansatz has
just been applied. In a final step we extend our proof by allowing for
time-dependent and multi-dimensional parameters as well as for network
topologies other than global coupling. This renders OA ansatz excellent
starting point for the analysis of broad class of realistic settings.

We present a simple method to solve spherical harmonics moment systems, such
as the the time-dependent $P_N$ and $SP_N$ equations, of radiative transfer.
The method, which works for arbitrary moment order $N$, makes use of the
specific coupling between the moments in the $P_N$ equations. This coupling
naturally induces staggered grids in space and time, which in turn give rise to
a canonical, second-order accurate finite difference scheme. While the scheme
does not possess TVD or realizability limiters, its simplicity allows for a
very efficient implementation in Matlab. We present several test cases, some of
which demonstrate that the code solves problems with ten million degrees of
freedom in space, angle, and time within a few seconds. The code for the
numerical scheme, called StaRMAP (Staggered grid Radiation Moment
Approximation), along with files for all presented test cases, can be
downloaded so that all results can be reproduced by the reader.

Recently, Deep-Neural-Network (DNN) based edge prediction is progressing
rapidly. While the DNN based schemes outperform the conventional edge detectors,
they have much greater theoretical complexity. It may be that the DNN based
edge sensors also adopt the neural net structures used for high-level
computer vision functions, such as image segmentation and object recognition. Edge
detection is a fairly local and easy job, the over-complicated design
and massive parameters would be excessive. Instead, we propose a traditional
method inspired framework to produce good edges with minimum complexity. We
simplify the network design to include Feature Extractor, Enrichment, and
Summarizer, which approximately correspond to gradient, high pass filtering, and pixel
connection in the typical edge detection schemes. The proposed structure
can thus improve the complexity and retain the edge prediction quality.
Our TIN2 (Traditional Inspired Networks) model has an accuracy greater than the
previous BDCN2 (Bi-Directional Cascade Networks) but with a narrower model.

This paper presents an efficient labeling procedure and its application to the real-time semantic segmentation of the environment with a narrow-beam swept-frequency, continuous-wave (Frequency Modulated Continuous-Wave) scanning-radiometry system. It is recommended to use this technology over the other standard means of spatial environment characterization, because it operates at a greater range and is much more tolerant of atmospheric conditions. The training procedure is based on a publicly available and state-of-the-art natural image segmentation system and, in contrast to previous approaches, enables the generation of rich labels for the incoming data stream by integrating four image and two LiDAR data streams. Furthermore, the radial losses are computed by accumulating the LiDAR returns along a pose-chain in front of and behind the current position of the vehicle. Finally, the network is presented with multi-channel inputs from the incoming scans of the environment.

This paper presents a method for measuring the squeezed vacuum state using a bichromatic local oscillator. The squeezed vacuum state is a quantum state of light that exhibits reduced quantum noise in one quadrature compared to the vacuum state. The authors propose a setup that combines a squeezed vacuum state with a bichromatic local oscillator to measure the squeezing parameter. They demonstrate the effectiveness of their method through experimental results, showing a high degree of accuracy in measuring the squeezing parameter. This measurement technique has potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum communication.

We define a class of groups equipped with an invariant probability measure,
which includes all compact groups and is closed under taking ultraproducts with
the induced Loeb measure; in fact, this class also contains the ultraproducts
all locally compact unimodular amenable groups. We call the members of this
class probability groups and develop the basics of the theory of their
measure-preserving actions on probability spaces, including a natural notion of
mixing. A short proof reveals that for probability groups mixing implies double
recurrence, which generalizes a theorem of Bergelson and Tao proved for
ultraproducts of finite groups. Moreover, a quantitative version of our proof
gives that $\varepsilon$-approximate mixing implies
$3\sqrt{\varepsilon}$-approximate double recurrence. Examples of approximately
mixing probability groups are quasirandom groups introduced by Gowers, so the
last theorem generalizes and sharpens the corresponding results for quasirandom
groups of Bergelson and Tao, as well as of Austin. Lastly, we point out that
the fact that the ultraproduct of locally compact unimodular amenable groups is
a probability group provides a general alternative to Furstenberg
correspondence principle.

Conditional generative flow models have shown promising results in generating high-quality images and 3D point clouds. However, existing methods often suffer from limitations such as limited expressiveness and difficulty in handling complex conditional distributions. In this paper, we propose C-Flow, a novel conditional generative flow model that addresses these limitations. C-Flow leverages the invertible architecture of flow models and introduces conditional coupling layers to model complex conditional distributions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of C-Flow on various image and 3D point cloud datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of both visual quality and quantitative metrics. Additionally, we conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components in C-Flow and provide insights into its working mechanism. Overall, our work contributes to the advancement of conditional generative flow models and opens up new possibilities for generating realistic images and 3D point clouds.

Morphological reconstruction (MR) is often employed by seeded image
segmentation algorithms such as watershed transform and power watershed as it
is able to filter seeds (regional minima) to reduce over-segmentation. However,
MR might mistakenly filter meaningful seeds that are required for generating
accurate segmentation and it is also sensitive to the scale because a
single-scale structuring element is employed. In this paper, a novel adaptive
morphological reconstruction (AMR) operation is proposed that has three
advantages. Firstly, AMR can adaptively filter useless seeds while preserving
meaningful ones. Secondly, AMR is insensitive to the scale of structuring
elements because multiscale structuring elements are employed. Finally, AMR has
two attractive properties: monotonic increasingness and convergence that help
seeded segmentation algorithms to achieve a hierarchical segmentation.
Experiments clearly demonstrate that AMR is useful for improving algorithms of
seeded image segmentation and seed-based spectral segmentation. Compared to
several state-of-the-art algorithms, the proposed algorithms provide better
segmentation results requiring less computing time. Source code is available at
https://github.com/SUST-reynole/AMR.

This paper presents a deep learning  approach for  multi-task medical image segmentation in multiple modalities. The proposed method utilizes a   convolutional neural network  (CNN) architecture that is capable  of simultaneously segmenting multiple anatomical structures in different imaging modalities. The network is  trained  using a  combination of supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, allowing it  to learn from  both labeled and unlabeled data.  Experimental results on a  large dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, achieving  state-of-the-art  performance in multi-task medical  image segmentation across multiple modalities.  The proposed  approach  has the potential to improve  the accuracy and efficiency of medical  image  analysis, leading to better diagnosis and treatment planning in clinical practice.

We extend the well-known cont-Bouchaud model to include a hierarchical
topology of agent's interactions. The influence of hierarchy on system dynamics
is investigated by two models. The first one is based on A Multi-level, nested
Erdos-Renyi random graph and individual decisions by agents according to Potts
dynamics. This approach does not lead to a broad return distribution outside a
Parameter regime close to the original Cont-Bouchaud model. In the second model
we introduce a limited hierarchical Erdos-Renyi graph, where merging of
clusters at a level h+1 involves only clusters that have merged at the previous
level h and we use the original Cont-Bouchaud agent dynamics on resulting
Clusters. The second model leads to a heavy-tail distribution of cluster sizes
and relative price changes in a wide Range of connection densities, not only
close to the percolation threshold.

This paper investigates the homology cycles in manifolds with locally standard torus actions. The authors define a notion of homology cycles for such manifolds and study their properties. They show that the set of homology cycles forms a lattice structure and provide a characterization of the minimal and maximal elements in this lattice. The authors also establish a connection between homology cycles and equivariant cohomology, and use this connection to compute the homology cycles for certain classes of manifolds. Overall, this paper provides a comprehensive study of homology cycles in manifolds with locally standard torus actions and contributes to our understanding of the topology of these manifolds.

We investigate the prospects and consequences of the spectral level
reconstruction of primordial $B$-mode power by solving the systems of linear
equations assuming that the lensing potential together with the lensed
polarization spectra are already in hand. We find that this reconstruction
technique may be very useful to have an estimate of the amplitude of primordial
gravity waves or more specifically the value of tensor to scalar ratio. We also
see that one can have cosmic variance limited reconstruction of the intrinsic
$B$-mode power up to few hundred multipoles ($\ell\sim500$) which is more than
sufficient to have an estimate of the tensor to scalar ratio. Since the small
scale cosmic microwave background (CMB henceforth) anisotropies are not sourced
by the primordial gravity waves generated during inflation. We also find that
the impact of instrumental noise may be bypassed within this reconstruction
algorithm. A simple demonstration for the nullification of the instrumental
noise anticipating COrE like futuristic space mission complemented with Planck
2013 cosmology has been presented.

Let A be an arbitrary integral domain of characteristic 0 which is finitely
generated over Z. We consider Thue equations $F(x,y)=b$ with unknowns x,y from
A and hyper- and superelliptic equations $f(x)=by^m$ with unknowns from A,
where the binary form F and the polynomial f have their coefficients in A,
where b is a non-zero element from A, and where m is an integer at least 2.
Under the necessary finiteness conditions imposed on F,f,m, we give explicit
upper bounds for the sizes of x,y in terms of suitable representations for
A,F,f,b Our results imply that the solutions of Thue equations and hyper- and
superelliptic equations over arbitrary finitely generated domains can be
determined effectively in principle. Further, we generalize a theorem of
Schinzel and Tijdeman to the effect, that there is an effectively computable
constant C such that $f(x)=by^m$ has no solutions in x,y from A with y not 0 or
a root of unity if m>C. In our proofs, we use effective results for Thue
equations and hyper- and superelliptic equations over number fields and
function fields, some effective commutative algebra, and a specialization
argument.

Adaptive networks are a suitable choice for decentralized inference tasks, such as for monitoring complex natural phenomena. Recent works have been focused on the case where the nodes estimate a single optimum parameter vector in a collective manner. However, many important applications are multi-problem-oriented, in the sense that the network has to estimate simultaneously a set of optimum parameters, distributed over the area covered by the network. In this paper, we employ diffusion strategies to develop distributed algorithms that can handle such a situation by minimizing a suitable squared error criterion, using a 2-regularized criterion. The convergence properties of the proposed approach are analyzed and experimentally verified. Moreover, we use simulations to illustrate the use of the proposed method in several applications involving hyperspectral sensing, localization and unmixing.

There is large consent that successful training of deep networks requires
many thousand annotated training samples. In this paper, we present a network
and training strategy that relies on the strong use of data augmentation to use
the available annotated samples more efficiently. The architecture consists of
a contracting path to capture context and symmetric expanding path that
enables precise localization. We show that such a network can be trained
end-to-end from very few images and outperforms prior best method (a
sliding-window convolutional network) on ISBI challenge for segmentation of
neuronal structures in electron microscopic stacks. Using the same network
trained on transmitted light microscopy images (phase contrast and DIC) we won
the ISBI cell tracking challenge 2015 in these categories by large margin.
Moreover, the network is fast. Segmentation of a 512x512 image takes less than
a second on recent GPU. The full implementation (based on Caffe) and the
trained networks are available at
http://lmb.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/people/ronneber/u-net .

Algebraic multigrid (AMG) methods have been widely used to solve linear systems arising in particle methods. However, most of the existing literature focuses on symmetric matrices. In this paper, we investigate the performance of AMG methods for non-symmetric matrices arising in particle methods. Specifically, we consider two types of non-symmetric matrices: those corresponding to the connections between particles in physical space and those corresponding to the connections between particles in parameter space. We compare the performance of two popular AMG methods, namely smoothed aggregation (SA) and algebraic multigrid (AMG), on a set of test problems. Our results show that SA outperforms AMG for both types of non-symmetric matrices, highlighting the importance of considering non-symmetric matrices in the design of AMG methods for particle methods. We also provide some insights into the reasons behind the observed performance differences. Overall, this paper contributes to a better understanding of the performance of AMG methods for non-symmetric matrices in particle methods and provides guidance for selecting appropriate AMG methods in practice.

In this study, a machine learning algorithm is used for disaggregation of
SMAP brightness temperatures (T$_{\textrm{B}}$) from 36km to 9km. It uses image
segmentation to clustre the study region based on meteorological and land cover
similarity, followed by a support vector machine based regression that computes
the value of the disaggregated T$_{\textrm{B}}$ at all pixels. High resolution
remote sensing products such as land surface temperature, normalised difference
vegetation index, enhanced vegetation index, precipitation, soil texture, and
land-cover were used for disaggregation. The algorithm was implemented in Iowa,
United States, from April to July 2015, and compared with the SMAP L3_SM_AP
T$_{\textrm{B}}$ product at 9km. It was found that the disaggregated
T$_{\textrm{B}}$ were very similar to the SMAP-T$_{\textrm{B}}$ product, even
for vegetated areas with a mean difference $\leq$ 5K. However, the standard
deviation of the disaggregation was lower by 7K than that of the AP product.
The probability density functions of the disaggregated T$_{\textrm{B}}$ were
similar to the SMAP-T$_{\textrm{B}}$. The results indicate that this algorithm
may be used for disaggregating T$_{\textrm{B}}$ using complex non-linear
correlations on a grid.

The segmentation of animals from camera-trap images is a difficult task. To
illustrate, there are various challenges due to environmental conditions and
hardware limitation in these images. We proposed a multi-layer robust principal
component analysis (multi-layer RPCA) approach for background subtraction. Our
method computes sparse and low-rank images from a weighted sum of descriptors,
using colour and texture features as case of study for camera-trap images
segmentation. The segmentation algorithm is composed of histogramme equalisation
or Gaussian philtreing as pre-processing, and morphological philtres with active
contour as post-processing. The parametres of our multi-layer RPCA were
optimised with an exhaustive search. The database consists of camera-trap
images from the Colombian forest taken by the Instituto de Investigaci\'on de
Recursos Biol\'ogicos Alexander von Humboldt. We analysed the performance of
our method in inherent and therefore challenging situations of camera-trap
images. Furthermore, we compared our method with some state-of-the-art
algorithms of background subtraction, where our multi-layer RPCA outperformed
these other methods. Our multi-layer RPCA reached 76.17 and 69.97% of average
fine-grained F-measure for colour and infrared sequences, respectively. To our
best knowledge, this paper is the first work proposing multi-layer RPCA and
using it for camera-trap images segmentation.

Most existing black-box optimization methods assume that all variables in the
system being optimized have equal cost and can change freely at each iteration.
However, in many real world systems, inputs are passed through a sequence of
different operations or modules, making variables in earlier stages of
processing more costly to update. Such structure imposes a cost on switching
variables in early parts of a data processing pipeline. In this work, we
propose a new algorithm for switch cost-aware optimization called Lazy Modular
Bayesian Optimization (LaMBO). This method efficiently identifies the global
optimum while minimizing cost through a passive change of variables in early
modules. The method is theoretical grounded and achieves vanishing regret when
augmented with switching cost. We apply LaMBO to multiple synthetic functions
and a three-stage image segmentation pipeline used in a neuroscience
application, where we obtain promising improvements over prevailing cost-aware
Bayesian optimization algorithms. Our results demonstrate that LaMBO is an
effective strategy for black-box optimization that is capable of minimizing
switching costs in modular systems.

We consider two ensembles of nxn matrices. The first is the set of all nxn
matrices with entries zeroes and ones such that all column sums and all row
sums equal r, uniformly weighted. The second is the set of nxn matrices with
zero and one entries where the probability that any given entry is one is r/n,
the probabilities of the set of individual entries being i.i.d.'s. Calling the
two expectation values E and EB respectively, we develop a formal relation
E(perm(A)) = EB(perm (A)) x exp{sum Ti}. We also use a well-known approximating
ensemble to E, E1. We prove using E or E1 one obtains the same value of Ti for
i < 21. (THE PUBLISHED VERSION OF THIS PAPER ONLY OBTAINS RESULTS FOR i < 8. We
go beyond the results of the published version by taking much more advantage of
recent work of Pernici and of Wanless on i-matchings on regular bipartite
graphs.)These terms Ti, i < 21, have amazing properties. We conjecture that
these properties hold also for all i.

Deep Learning is considered to be a quite young in area of machine
learning research, found its effectiveness in dealing complex yet high
dimensional dataset that includes but limited to images, text and speech etc.
with multiple levels of representation and abstraction. As there are plethora
of research on these datasets by various researchers , win over them needs
lots of attention. Careful setting of Deep learning parameters is of paramount
importance in order to avoid overfitting unlike conventional methods with
limited parameter settings. Deep Convolutional neural network (DCNN) with
multiple layers of compositions and appropriate settings might be is an
efficient machine learning method that can outperform conventional methods
in a great way. However, due to its slow adoption in learning, there are also
always a chance of overfitting during feature selection process, which can be
addressed by employing a regularization method called dropout. Fast Random
Forest (FRF) is powerful ensemble classifier especially when datasets are
noisy and when the number of attributes is large in comparison to number of
instances, as is the case of Bioinformatics datasets. Several publicly
available Bioinformatics dataset, Handwritten digits recognition and Image
segmentation dataset are considered for evaluation of proposed approach.
The excellent performance obtained by the proposed DCNN based feature selection
with FRF classifier on high dimensional datasets makes it a fast and accurate
classifier in comparison the state-of-the-art.

As a natural way for human-computer interaction, fixation provides a
promising solution for interactive image segmentation. In this paper, we focus
on Personal Fixations-based Object Segmentation (PFOS) to adress issues in
previous studies, such as the lack of appropriate dataset and the ambiguity in
fixations-based interaction. In particular, we first construct a new PFOS
dataset by carefully collecting pixel-level binary annotation data over an
existing fixation prediction dataset, such dataset is expected to greatly
facilitate the study along the line. Then, considering characteristics of
personal fixations, we propose a novel network based on Object Localization and
Boundary Preservation (OLBP) to segment the gazed objects. Specifically, the
OLBP network utilizes an Object Localization Module (OLM) to analyze personal
fixations and locates the gazed objects based on the interpretation. Then, a
Boundary Preservation Module (BPM) is designed to introduce additional boundary
information to guard the completeness of the gazed objects. Moreover, OLBP is
organized in the mixed bottom-up and top-down manner with multiple types of
deep supervision. Extensive experiments on the constructed PFOS dataset show
the superiority of the proposed OLBP network over 17 state-of-the-art methods,
and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed OLM and BPM components. The
constructed PFOS dataset and the proposed OLBP network are available at
https://github.com/MathLee/OLBPNet4PFOS.

This paper presents a novel approach for neuron segmentation in electron microscopy (EM) images using learning metric graphs. Neuron segmentation is a crucial step in understanding the structure and connectivity of neural circuits. Traditional methods for neuron segmentation rely on manual annotation or thresholding techniques, which are time-consuming and prone to errors. In this work, we propose a learning-based approach that leverages the power of metric graphs to accurately segment neurons in EM images. We first construct a graph representation of the image, where each node corresponds to a pixel and edges represent the similarity between pixels. We then learn a metric on this graph using a deep neural network, which captures the underlying structure of the neurons. Finally, we use this learned metric to perform graph-based segmentation, where nodes are grouped into connected components corresponding to individual neurons. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. Our method has the potential to significantly advance the field of connectomics by enabling automated and accurate segmentation of neurons in large-scale EM images.

Dilated convolutions are widely used in deep semantic segmentation models as
they can enlarge the filters' receptive field without adding additional weights
nor sacrificing spatial resolution. However, as dilated convolutional filters
do not possess positional knowledge about the pixels on semantically meaningful
contours, they could lead to ambiguous predictions on object boundaries. In
addition, although dilating the filter can expand its receptive field, the
total number of sampled pixels remains unchanged, which usually comprises a
small fraction of the receptive field's total area. Inspired by the Lateral
Inhibition (LI) mechanisms in human visual systems, we propose the dilated
convolution with lateral inhibitions (LI-Convs) to overcome these limitations.
Introducing LI mechanisms improves the convolutional filter's sensitivity to
semantic object boundaries. Moreover, since LI-Convs also implicitly take the
pixels from the laterally inhibited zones into consideration, they can also
extract features at a denser scale. By integrating LI-Convs into the Deeplabv3+
architecture, we propose the Lateral Inhibited Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling
(LI-ASPP), the Lateral Inhibited MobileNet-V2 (LI-MNV7) and the Lateral
Inhibited ResNet (LI-ResNet). Experimental results on three benchmark datasets
(PASCAL VOC 8147, CelebAMask-HQ and ADE20K) show that our LI-based segmentation
models outperform the baseline on all of them, thus verify the effectiveness
and generality of the proposed LI-Convs.

Flow-based generative models have highly desirable properties  like exact
log-likelihood evaluation and exact latent-variable inference, however they are
still  in their infancy and have not received as  much attention as alternative
generative models. In this paper, we introduce C-Flow, a novel  conditioning
scheme that brings normalizing flows to an entirely new  scenario with  great
possibilities for multi-modal data modeling. C-Flow is  based on  a  parallel
sequence of  invertible mappings in which a source flow  guides the target flow
at  every  step,  enabling fine-grained control over the generation process. We
also devise a new strategy to model unordered  3D  point clouds that, in
combination with the conditioning scheme, makes it  possible to address 3D
reconstruction from a single  image and its inverse  problem  of  rendering an
image  given a  point cloud. We demonstrate  our conditioning method  to be very
adaptable, being also applicable to image manipulation, style  transfer and
multi-modal image-to-image mapping  in a diversity   of  domains, including RGB
images, segmentation maps, and edge masks.

This paper presents a theoretical framework for understanding unconventional superconductivity in strongly correlated systems. The authors propose a real space pairing mechanism, which takes into account the strong electron-electron interactions present in these systems. They also develop a statistically consistent mean-field theory to describe the behavior of the superconducting state. The paper provides a comprehensive perspective on the current understanding of unconventional superconductivity and offers insights into the underlying physics of these systems.

This paper presents a novel approach for integrating inference and learning of neural factors in structural support vector machines (SVMs). The proposed method combines the strengths of both neural networks and SVMs to improve the performance of structured prediction tasks. The authors introduce a new neural factorization model that allows for efficient inference and learning of neural factors in SVMs. They demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach on several benchmark datasets and compare it to existing methods. The results show that the integrated inference and learning of neural factors in SVMs outperforms other approaches in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Overall, this paper provides a valuable contribution to the field of structured prediction and highlights the potential of combining neural networks and SVMs for improved performance.

This paper investigates the transition of Charlier polynomials to the Hermite function. Charlier polynomials are a family of orthogonal polynomials that arise in the study of quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics. The Hermite function, on the other hand, is a special function that is widely used in various areas of mathematics and physics. The paper presents a detailed analysis of the relationship between Charlier polynomials and the Hermite function, including their respective properties and applications. The results of this study provide valuable insights into the mathematical and physical connections between these two important mathematical objects.

This paper presents a non-parametric convolution based image-segmentation method for ill-posed objects using a context window approach. The proposed method aims to overcome the challenges of segmenting objects with complex shapes and unclear boundaries. The method utilizes a convolution operation to extract local features from the image and applies a context window approach to incorporate global information. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in accurately segmenting ill-posed objects. The proposed method shows promising potential for applications in computer vision and image processing tasks.

This paper proposes a novel approach for nuclear segmentation in digital pathology images using sparse coding driven deep decision tree ensembles. The proposed method combines the advantages of sparse coding and deep decision tree ensembles to achieve accurate and efficient nuclear segmentation. The sparse coding technique is used to learn a set of discriminative features from the input images, which are then fed into a deep decision tree ensemble for classification. Experimental results on a large dataset of digital pathology images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed method has the potential to significantly improve the performance of nuclear segmentation in digital pathology, which is a critical task in cancer diagnosis and treatment.

This paper presents a method for correcting timing jitter in a Ti:sapphire laser system used for pump-probe experiments in a free-electron laser (FEL) facility. The timing jitter of the laser system is measured using a jitter measurement system, and a correction algorithm is developed based on this measurement. The algorithm is implemented in real-time using a field-programmable gate array (FPGA), allowing for femtosecond resolution timing jitter correction. The effectiveness of the correction algorithm is demonstrated through experimental measurements, showing a significant reduction in timing jitter and improved stability of the laser system. This work provides a valuable tool for improving the performance of Ti:sapphire laser systems used in FEL pump-probe experiments, enabling more precise measurements and increasing the capabilities of FEL facilities.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach to solving the self-repelling snake model using the Split Bregman algorithm. The self-repelling snake model is a widely used method for image segmentation, but it suffers from slow convergence and sensitivity to initialization. The Split Bregman algorithm, on the other hand, is a powerful optimization technique that has been successfully applied to various image processing problems. We demonstrate that by incorporating the Split Bregman algorithm into the self-repelling snake model, we can significantly improve its convergence speed and robustness to initialization. We provide experimental results on various image datasets to validate the effectiveness of our proposed approach. Our findings suggest that the Split Bregman algorithm can be a valuable tool for solving the self-repelling snake model and improving the accuracy of image segmentation.

The Third Gravitational Lensing Accuracy Testing (GREAT3) Challenge is a collaborative effort to assess the accuracy of different methods for measuring weak gravitational lensing. This field of research is important for understanding the distribution of matter in the universe and testing theories of gravity. The challenge consists of simulated images of galaxies that have been lensed by the gravitational pull of foreground dark matter structures. Participants are tasked with accurately measuring the shapes of these galaxies and inferring the underlying dark matter distribution. This handbook provides a comprehensive overview of the challenge, including the motivation, methodology, and evaluation metrics. It also includes a detailed description of the simulation tools and data products that have been developed for the challenge. The handbook is intended to serve as a resource for participants and to facilitate the interpretation of challenge results.

Interactive video object segmentation involves the task of accurately segmenting objects  of  interest in video  sequences. While extensive research has been done on  this  topic, most existing methods have focused  on static images   and lack the ability  to handle videos in real-time. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for  interactive  video object segmentation in the wild,  which combines both image-based and video-based segmentation techniques. We introduce a user-guided interactive process that allows users to provide initial object masks and refine the segmentation  over time.  Our method leverages both spatial  and   temporal  information  to improve  segmentation accuracy  and handles challenging  conditions such as occlusions and moving backgrounds. We  evaluate our approach on a  large-scale dataset and demonstrate its effectiveness in various scenarios. The  results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance  in terms of accuracy and  speed,  making it a  valuable tool for interactive video  object segmentation in real-world applications.

We analyze performance of a linear-equality-constrained least-squares
(CLS) algorithm and its relaxed version, called rCLS, that is obtained via the
method of weighting. The rCLS algorithm solves unconstrained least-squares
problem that is augmented by incorporating a weighted form of linear
constraints. As result, unlike the CLS algorithm, rCLS algorithm is
amenable to our approach to performance analysis presented here, which is akin
to the energy-conservation-based methodology. Therefore, we initially inspect
the convergence properties and evaluate the precision of estimation as well as
satisfaction of the constraints for rCLS algorithm in both mean and
mean-square senses. Afterwards, we examine the performance of CLS algorithm
by evaluating the limiting performance of rCLS algorithm as the relaxation
parameter (weight) approaches infinity. Numerical examples verify accuracy
of the theoretical findings.

Analyzing the exchange energy of two conduction electrons in a crystal we
find that the exchange energy may be negative and, thus, a singlet state may be
favourable. A full overlap in real space of wave functions of two conduction
electrons leads to a deeper exchange energy. Thus, the exchange interaction
causes a bond between two conduction electrons in real space. The singlet bond
is possible because the singlet electrons can simultaneously and permanently
occupy one spatial ground state, so the average energy of paired electrons is
lower than the energy of unpaired electrons. Thus, the pairing is a result of
the Pauli Exclusion Principle. If conduction electrons, before pairing, are put
on the Fermi surface in the momentum space, then every pair may exist
permanently in time. The motion of conduction electrons in the crystal may
prevent the formation of Cooper pairs, because the kinetic energy of the motion
is usually larger than the binding energy in the pair. Conduction electrons as
standing waves are local and have zero momenta, hence their momenta are
synchronous; therefore, weak singlet bonds are stable despite the large kinetic
energy on the Fermi surface. The local pairing of standing waves explains the
inverse isotope effect, Tc-dome, insulator-superconductor transitions and many
other facts about superconductors. The electron pairs, as bosons, can form a
macroscopically coherent Bose-Einstein-Condensate and, thus, become
non-dissipative and non-local.

This paper presents a novel approach to active learning for medical image segmentation, with the goal of reducing uncertainty within the training pool. The proposed method utilizes a combination of uncertainty sampling and query-by-committee techniques to select the most informative samples for annotation. The uncertainty of each sample is estimated using a deep neural network, which is trained on a small initial labeled dataset. The selected samples are then annotated by experts and added to the training set, iteratively improving the segmentation model. Experimental results on a dataset of medical images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms traditional random sampling and achieves comparable performance to fully supervised learning with a significantly smaller labeled dataset. The findings of this study have implications for improving the efficiency and accuracy of medical image segmentation tasks.

Vision Transformers  (ViTs) have recently emerged as a powerful approach for image classification tasks. However, training ViTs effectively requires careful  consideration of data,  augmentation, and regularization techniques. In  this paper, we investigate the impact  of different data  strategies, augmentation methods, and regularization techniques on the performance  of ViTs. We conduct  extensive experiments  on various  benchmark  datasets   and analyze the  results to  provide insights into the best practices  for training ViTs. Our findings demonstrate the importance of large-scale datasets, diverse augmentation techniques, and  regularization methods such  as dropout and weight decay. We also propose a novel regularization technique called patch-level dropout, which improves the performance of ViTs by encouraging the model to attend to different parts of the  image.  Overall, our   study provides valuable guidelines for   training ViTs and sheds light on the  factors that  contribute to  their success in image  classification tasks.

This paper examines the consistency of matter models with asymptotically safe quantum gravity. The authors argue that matter models that are required to be consistent with asymptotically safe quantum gravity should satisfy certain conditions. These conditions include the asymptotic safety condition, the effective average action, and the gravitational coupling. The authors analyze various matter models, such as scalar fields, gauge fields, and fermions, and determine whether they satisfy these conditions. They also discuss the implications of consistent matter models for the UV behavior of quantum gravity and the renormalization group flow. Overall, the paper concludes that certain matter models are consistent with asymptotically safe quantum gravity and provide important insights into the UV behavior of the theory. This has significant implications for the field of quantum gravity and the understanding of the fundamental nature of matter.

This paper presents a novel approach to fundus image segmentation using a combination of boundary and entropy-driven adversarial learning. The proposed method incorporates both the boundary information and the entropy of the predicted segmentation maps to guide the training process. An adversarial network is designed to generate more accurate and realistic segmentations by minimizing the difference between the real and generated segmentation maps. The experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness in fundus image segmentation tasks. This work contributes to the advancement of medical image analysis and can potentially improve the diagnosis and treatment of various eye diseases.

This academic paper titled "Face Identification with Second-Order Pooling" presents a novel approach to face identification using second-order pooling. Traditional face identification methods rely on first-order pooling techniques, which may not effectively capture the rich spatial relationships between facial features. In this paper, we propose a second-order pooling method that aggregates high-dimensional feature vectors into a low-dimensional representation. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves superior face identification accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the performance of our method across various datasets and discuss its potential applications in facial recognition systems. Overall, our proposed second-order pooling technique offers a promising approach to enhancing face identification accuracy and has the potential for broad practical applications.

Over the past few years it has been demonstrated that "coarse timesteppers"
establish a link between traditional numerical analysis and microscopic/
stochastic simulation. The underlying assumption of the associated
lift-run-restrict-estimate procedure is that macroscopic models exist and close
in terms of a few governing moments of microscopically evolving distributions,
but they are unavailable in closed form. This leads to a system identification
based computational approach that sidesteps the necessity of deriving explicit
closures. Two-level codes are constructed; the outer code performs macroscopic,
continuum level numerical tasks, while the inner code estimates -through
appropriately initialized bursts of microscopic simulation- the quantities
required for continuum numerics. Such quantities include residuals, time
derivatives, and the action of coarse slow Jacobians. We demonstrate how these
coarse timesteppers can be applied to perform equation-free computations of a
kinetic Monte Carlo simulation of E. coli chemotaxis. Coarse-grained
contraction mappings, system level stability analysis as well as acceleration
of the direct simulation, are enabled through this computational multiscale
enabling technology.

In this paper, we adopt 3D Convolutional Neural Networks to segment
volumetric medical images. Although deep neural networks have been proven to be
very effective on many 2D vision tasks, it is still challenging to apply them
to 3D tasks due to the limited amount of annotated 3D data and limited
computational resources. We propose a novel 3D-based coarse-to-fine framework
to effectively and efficiently tackle these challenges. The proposed 3D-based
framework outperforms the 2D counterpart to a large margin since it can
leverage the rich spatial infor- mation along all three axees. We conduct
experiments on two datasets which include healthy and pathological pancreases
