The Elementary Cycle Theory correctly describes elementary quanta as the manifestation of the most rapid rotational dynamics of space and time, which is, however, classical in essence. Its special relativistic geometrodynamics offers a de facto unified view of ordinary relativistic and quantum physics. In particular, its classical-relativistic cyclic dynamics precisely reproduces from the classical first principles all the most basic aspects of quantum mechanics, such as all its axioms, the Feynman path integral, the Dirac-Dirac quantization (second quantization), the quantum dynamics of statistical systems, the non-relativistic quanta, atoms, superconductivity, graphene physics, etc. Furthermore, it allows a direct derivation of the gauge transformations of the gauge invariance without any further assumption, in a direct analogy to the description of the gravitational interaction in general relativity. In this paper we summarize some of the major achievements of this new formulation of the quantum-particle physics, which have been proven by a series of recent peer-reviewed papers.

In medical image segmentation tasks, multi-atlas segmentation has become a popular approach due to its accuracy and robustness. However, the traditional label fusion methods used in multi-atlas segmentation suffer from limitations in cases of severe noise or outliers. In this paper, we propose a novel deep learning-based label fusion method called VoteNet. VoteNet incorporates a deep convolutional neural network architecture and a voting strategy to aggregate multiple label predictions from different atlases. Experimental results on a benchmark dataset demonstrate that VoteNet achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art label fusion methods, even in the presence of noise and outliers. Our proposed method has the potential to improve the accuracy and reliability of multi-atlas segmentation in various medical imaging applications.

We propose a novel attention gate (AG) Model for medical imaging that
automatically learns to focus on target structures of varying shapes and sizes.
Models trained with AGs implicitly learn to suppress irrelevant regions in an
input image while highlighting salient features useful for a specific Task.
This enables us to eliminate the necessity of using explicit external
tissue/organ localisation modules of cascaded convolutional neural networks
(CNNs). AGs Can Be easily integrated into standard CNN architectures such as
the u-Net model with minimal computational overhead while Increasing the model
Sensitivity and prediction accuracy. The proposed Attention U-Net architecture
is evaluated on two large CT abdominal datasets for multi-class image
segmentation. Experimental results show that AGs consistently improve the
prediction performance of U-Net across different datasets and training sizes
while preserving computational efficiency. The code for the proposed
architecture is publicly available.

In this work, we propose an adaptive spectral element algorithm for solving
nonlinear optimal control problems. The method employs orthogonal collocation
at the shifted Gegenbauer-Gauss points combined with very accurate and stable
numerical quadratures to fully discretize the multiple-phase integral form of
the optimal control problem. The proposed algorithm relies on exploiting the
underlying smoothness properties of the solutions for computing approximate
solutions efficiently. In particular, the method brackets discontinuities and
"points of nonsmoothness" through a novel local adaptive algorithm, which
achieves a desired accuracy on the discrete dynamical system equations by
adjusting both the mesh size and the degree of the approximating polynomials. A
rigorous error analysis of the developed numerical quadratures is presented.
Finally, the efficiency of the proposed method is demonstrated on three test
examples from the open literature.

Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) are powerful sources of radiation found at the centers of galaxies. They are believed to be powered by accretion of matter onto supermassive black holes. This paper provides an overview of AGN, including their classification, physical properties, and observational characteristics. The different types of AGN, such as quasars, Seyfert galaxies, and blazars, are discussed, along with their unique features and emission mechanisms. The paper also explores the role of AGN in galaxy evolution and their connection to other astrophysical phenomena, such as jets and outflows. Finally, the current understanding of AGN physics and the challenges in studying these enigmatic objects are highlighted. Overall, this paper serves as a comprehensive introduction to the field of AGN research, providing a foundation for further investigation and exploration.

A right ideal (left ideal, two-sided ideal) is a non-empty language $L$ over
an alphabet $\Sigma$ such that $L=L\Sigma^*$ ($L=\Sigma^*R$,
$L=\Sigma^*L\Sigma^*$). Let $k=3$ for right ideals, 4 for right ideals and 5 for
two-sided ideals. We show that there exist sequences ($L_n \mid n \ge k $) of
right, left, and two-sided regular ideals, where $L_n$ has quotient complexity
(state complexity) $n$, such that $L_n$ is most complex in its class under the
following measures of complexity: the length of the syntactic semigroup, the
quotient complexities of the left quotients of $L_n$, the number of electrons
(intersections of complemented and uncomplemented left quotients), the quotient
complexities of the molecules, and the quotient complexities of reversal, star,
product (concatenation), and all binary boolean operations. In that sense,
these ideals are "most complex" languages in their classes, or "universal
witnesses" to the complexity of the various operations.

Semantic segmentation of medical images is   an essential first step in
computer-aided diagnosis systems for many applications. However, given many
disparate imaging modalities and inherent variations   in  the patient data, it is
difficult to consistently achieve high accuracy using modern deep neural
networks  (DNNs). This has  led researchers to propose interactive image
segmentation techniques  where  a medical expert can interactively correct the
output of   a DNN to  the desired accuracy. However, these  techniques often  need
separate training data  with  the associated human interactions, and do not
generalize to various diseases, and types of medical images.  In this paper, we
suggest a novel conditional  inference technique for DNNs which takes  the
intervention by a medical expert as test time constraints and performs
inference  conditioned upon these constraints. Our  technique is generic can be
used for medical images from any modality. Unlike other methods, our  approach
can correct multiple structures simultaneously and add structures  missed at
initial segmentation. We report an improvement of 13.3, 12.5, 17.8, 10.2, and
12.4 times in user annotation time than  full human  annotation for the nucleus,
multiple cells, liver and tumor, organ, and brain  segmentation  respectively. We
report  a time   saving  of 2.8, 3.0, 1.9, 4.4, and 8.6 fold compared  to   other
interactive segmentation  techniques. Our  method can be useful to clinicians for
diagnosis and post-surgical follow-up with  minimal  intervention from the
medical expert. The  source-code  and  the  detailed  results are available here
[1].

A variety of deep neural networks have been applied in medical image
segmentation and achieve good Performance. Unlike Natural images, medical
images of the same imaging modality are characterized by the same pattern,
which indicates that same normal organs or tissues locate at similar positions
in the images. Thus, in this paper we try to incorporate the prior knowledge of
Medical images into the structure of neural networks such that the prior
knowledge can be utilized for accurate segmentation. Based on this idea, we
propose a novel Deep network Called knowledge-based fully convolutional network
(KFCN) for medical image segmentation. The segmentation function and
corresponding error is analyzed. We show the existence of an asymptotically
stable region for KFCN which traditional FCN doesn't possess. Experiments
validate our knowledge assumption about The Incorporation of prior knowledge
into the convolution kernels of KFCN and show that KFCN can achieve a
reasonable segmentation and a satisfactory accuracy.

In Parity Games with costs, players aim to minimize their overall cost while trying to win the game. This paper presents an analysis of optimal strategies in such games and shows that finding an optimal strategy is computationally hard. The authors propose a new algorithm that combines techniques from game theory and linear programming to improve the efficiency of finding optimal strategies. The algorithm is tested on various benchmark games, and the results show that it outperforms existing approaches. Additionally, the paper provides theoretical insights into the complexity of finding optimal strategies in Parity Games with costs, thereby contributing to the understanding of this challenging problem.

Size uniformity is one of the main criteria of superpixel methods. But size
uniformity rarely conforms to the varying content of an image. The chosen size
of the superpixels therefore represents a compromise - how to obtain the fewest
superpixels without losing too much important detail. We propose that a more
appropriate criterion for creating image segments is information uniformity. We
introduce a novel method for segmenting an image based on this criterion. Since
information is a natural way of measuring image complexity, our proposed
algorithm leads to image segments that are smaller and denser in areas of high
complexity and larger in homogeneous regions, thus simplifying the image while
preserving its details. Our algorithm is simple and requires just one input
parameter - a threshold on the information content. On segmentation comparison
benchmarks it proves to be superior to the state-of-the-art. In addition, our
method is computationally very efficient, approaching real-time performance,
and is easily extensible to three-dimensional image stacks and video volumes.

The ability to detect change-points in a dynamic network or a time series of
graphs is an increasingly important task in many applications of the emerging
discipline of graph signal processing. This paper formulates change-point
detection as a hypothesis testing problem in terms of a generative latent
position model, focusing on the special case of the Stochastic Block Model time
series. We analyze two classes of scan statistics, based on distinct underlying
locality statistics presented in the literature. Our main contribution is the
derivation of the limiting distributions and power characteristics of the
competing scan statistics. Performance is compared theoretically, on synthetic
data, and on the Enron email corpus. We demonstrate that both statistics are
admissible in one simple setting, while one of the statistics is inadmissible a
second setting.

This paper presents a shape-aware semi-supervised approach for 3D semantic segmentation of medical images. The proposed method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to improve the segmentation accuracy. The shape information is incorporated into the segmentation process through a shape-aware regularization term, which encourages the segmentation to adhere to the underlying anatomical structures. The semi-supervised learning framework is formulated as a graph-based optimization problem, where the labeled and unlabeled data are represented as nodes in a graph and the segmentation labels are propagated through the graph using a diffusion process. Experimental results on a dataset of medical images demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy. The shape-aware regularization term effectively improves the segmentation quality by preserving the anatomical structures. The semi-supervised learning framework allows for better utilization of unlabeled data, leading to improved segmentation performance. Overall, the proposed method shows promise for accurate and efficient 3D semantic segmentation of medical images.

This paper  presents a variational image segmentation model that is coupled with  image restoration achievements. The   proposed model aims to simultaneously perform image segmentation   and restoration tasks by incorporating a  restoration term into the  energy functional  of the segmentation model. The restoration term is designed to  encourage smoothness  and preserve image details during the segmentation process. The proposed model is formulated  as an optimization problem, which is solved using an iterative algorithm. Experimental  results on  various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed   model compared   to existing methods in  terms of  segmentation accuracy and restoration quality. The proposed model has potential applications in various fields such as medical imaging, computer  vision, and remote   sensing.

This paper proposes a novel approach for initializing the weights of a deep neural network for image segmentation tasks using meta-learning. The authors argue that the choice of initial weights can greatly impact the performance of the network, and traditional random or pre-trained initializations may not be optimal for segmentation tasks. They introduce a meta-learning framework that learns to initialize the weights of the network based on the characteristics of the specific segmentation task. The proposed method is evaluated on several benchmark datasets and compared against traditional initialization methods. The results show that the meta-learned initializations consistently outperform the other methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the segmentation tasks. The authors conclude that meta-learning can be a powerful tool for improving the initialization of deep neural networks for image segmentation.

This paper addresses the issue of fast and accurate segmentation of pathological lung regions in medical images, which is crucial for diagnosis and treatment planning. The authors propose a novel near-optimal keypoint sampling method that improves the efficiency and accuracy of lung segmentation algorithms. The method uses a combination of keypoint detection and sampling techniques to identify and select the most informative keypoints on lung boundaries. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing sampling approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The near-optimal keypoint sampling method shows great potential for improving the performance of lung segmentation algorithms in medical image analysis.

This paper examines the dynamics and biases of online attention in the context of aircraft crashes. Using a large dataset of online news articles and social media posts, we analyze the patterns of attention towards aircraft crashes over a period of several years. We find that attention towards aircraft crashes is highly dynamic, with peaks of attention following major incidents and quickly declining afterwards. Furthermore, we identify several biases in the attention towards aircraft crashes, including a bias towards crashes involving commercial airlines and crashes with a high number of fatalities. These biases are influenced by various factors, such as media coverage and public perception of risk. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the dynamics and biases of online attention, and have implications for the dissemination of information and the perception of risk in the context of aircraft crashes.

In this paper, we study the properties of products of sequentially compact spaces, particularly their compactness with respect to a set of filters. We establish the necessary conditions for a product of sequentially compact spaces to be compact with respect to a set of filters generated by sets of the form {U(x)}x∈X, where U(x) is a neighborhood of x. We also investigate the relationship between compactness with respect to a set of filters and other notions of compactness. We provide several examples to illustrate the results and discuss their implications in various areas of mathematics. Finally, we conclude with some open questions and possible directions for future research.

White matter hyperintensity (WMH) is commonly found in elder individuals and
appears to be associated with brain diseases. U-net is a convolutional network
that has been widely used for biomedical image segmentation. Recently, U-net
has been successfully applied to WMH segmentation. Random initialization is
usally used to initialize the model weights in the U-net. 

However, the model
may coverage to different local optima with different randomly initialized
weights. 

We find a combination of thresholding and averaging the outputs of
U-nets with different random initializations can largely improve the WMH
segmentation accuracy. 

Based on this observation, we propose a post-processing
technique concerning the way how averaging and thresholding are conducted. Specifically, we first transfer the score maps from three U-nets to binary
masks via thresholding and then average those binary masks to obtain the final
WMH segmentation. 

Both quantitative analysis (via the Dice similarity
coefficient) and qualitative analysis (via visual examinations) reveal the
superior performance of the proposed method. 

This post-processing technique is
independent of the model used. As such, it can also be applied to situations
where other deep learning models are employed, especially when random
initialization is adopted and pre-training is unavailable.

This academic paper presents a study of the third unramified cohomology group of  universal torsors over rational surfaces. The authors investigate the structure  and properties of this cohomology group, focusing  on the  case of rational   surfaces.  They provide explicit  calculations and  examples, shedding  light on the  behavior of  the third unramified cohomology group in this particular setting. The results of this study  may have  implications for the understanding of torsors and their applications in algebraic geometry.

Transformer architecture has emerged to be successful in a number of natural
language processing tasks. However, its applications to  medical vision remain
largely unexplored. In this  study, we  present UTNet, a simple yet powerful
hybrid  Transformer architecture that integrates self-attention  into a
convolutional neural network  for enhancing medical image  segmentation. UTNet
applies self-attention modules in both encoder and decoder   for capturing
long-range dependency at  different scales with minimal overhead. To this end,
we  propose  an efficient self-attention mechanism along with relative position
encoding that reduces the complexity  of self-attention  operation significantly
from  $O(n^2)$ to approximate $O(n)$. A new self-attention decoder  is also
proposed to  recover fine-grained details   from the skipped connections in the
encoder. Our approach addresses the dilemma  that Transformer requires  huge
amounts of  data to  learn vision inductive  bias. Our hybrid layer design allows
the initialization of Transformer into convolutional  networks without a need  of
pre-training.  We have  evaluated UTNet on  the multi-label, multi-vendor cardiac
magnetic resonance imaging cohort.   UTNet  demonstrates superior segmentation
performance and robustness  against the state-of-the-art approaches, holding the
promise to generalize well on other medical image segmentations.
