This paper presents a performance analysis of an improved Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) Direction of Arrival (DoA) estimator. The proposed estimator incorporates a modified covariance matrix to enhance the accuracy of DoA estimation in the presence of noise and interference. The performance of the improved estimator is evaluated through simulations and compared with the conventional MUSIC algorithm. The results demonstrate that the proposed estimator achieves higher accuracy and robustness in estimating the DoA of multiple signals in various scenarios. The analysis provides valuable insights into the potential applications of the improved MUSIC DoA estimator in wireless communication systems and radar systems.

This paper proposes a novel approach for semantic image segmentation using loss max-pooling. The traditional max-pooling operation in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) is modified to incorporate loss information during training. The loss max-pooling operation selects the maximum value not only based on the input feature maps but also on the corresponding loss maps. This allows the network to focus on regions with high loss, improving the segmentation accuracy. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed loss max-pooling approach outperforms traditional max-pooling and other state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy. The proposed approach provides a promising direction for improving semantic image segmentation in CNNs.

Deep learning-based semi-supervised learning (SSL) algorithms have led to
promising results in medical images segmentation and can alleviate doctors'
expensive annotations by leveraging unlabeled data. However, most of the
existing SSL algorithms in literature tend to regularize the model training by
perturbing networks and/or data. Observing that multi/dual-task learning
attends to various levels of information which have inherent prediction
perturbation, we ask the question in this work: can we explicitly build
task-level regularization rather than implicitly constructing networks- and/or
data-level perturbation-and-transformation for SSL? To answer this question, we
propose a novel dual-task-consistency semi-supervised framework for the first
time. Concretely, we use a dual-task deep network that jointly predicts a
pixel-wise segmentation map and a geometry-aware level set representation of
the target. The level set representation is converted to an approximated
segmentation map through a differentiable task transform layer. Simultaneously,
we introduce a dual-task consistency regularization between the level
set-derived segmentation maps and directly predicted segmentation maps for both
labeled and unlabeled data. Extensive experiments on two public datasets show
that our method can largely improve the performance by incorporating the
unlabeled data. Meanwhile, our framework outperforms the state-of-the-art
semi-supervised medical image segmentation methods. Code is available at:
https://github.com/Luoxd1996/DTC

This paper provides a comprehensive historical survey of the various proofs of Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes, spanning from 300 B.C. to 2022. Euclid's theorem states that there are infinitely many prime numbers. The paper explores the development of different proofs throughout history, highlighting the advancements and insights made by mathematicians over the centuries. Additionally, the paper presents a new proof of Euclid's theorem, adding to the collection of existing proofs. The new proof contributes to the ongoing understanding and appreciation of this fundamental concept in number theory. Overall, this survey of proofs and the introduction of a new proof demonstrate the enduring significance and ongoing exploration of Euclid's theorem on the infinitude of primes.

Deep convolutional neural networks have shown outstanding performance in
medical image segmentation tasks. The usual problem when training supervised
deep learning methods is lack of labeled data which is time-consuming and
costly to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel uncertainty-guided
semi-supervised learning based on a student-teacher approach for training the
segmentation network using limited labeled samples and large number of
unlabeled images. First, teacher segmentation model is trained from the
labeled samples using Bayesian deep learning. The trained model is used to
generate soft segmentation labels and uncertainty maps for unlabeled set.
The student model is then updated using the softly segmented samples and the
corresponding pixel-wise confidence of segmentation quality estimated from
the uncertainty of the teacher model using a newly designed loss function.
Experimental results on retinal layer segmentation task show that the
proposed method improves segmentation performance in comparison to the
fully supervised approach and is on par with the expert annotator. The proposed
semi-supervised segmentation framework is a key contribution and applicable for
biomedical image segmentation across various imaging modalities where access to
annotated medical images is challenging

This paper demonstrates a tunable coupled-mode dispersion compensation technique for on-chip resonant four-wave mixing (FWM) applications. The proposed  technique involves designing and fabricating a  compact on-chip  waveguide structure  with  adjustable dispersion. The dispersion compensation is achieved  by integrating  a tunable  waveguide coupler and  a subwavelength grating coupler. The coupler is designed to have a variable coupling strength, allowing for adjustable dispersion compensation. The authors validate the functionality of the  tunable coupled-mode dispersion compensation  technique using  numerical simulations and present experimental results for on-chip FWM applications. The results show improved  FWM efficiency  and  enhanced dispersion management capabilities of  the  proposed  technique. This work provides valuable insights and potential applications for  on-chip  FWM  devices.

This paper presents a novel medical image segmentation model called w-Net, which incorporates multi-dimensional attention and cascade multi-scale convolution. The proposed model is trained using dual supervision, combining both pixel-level and region-level annotations. The multi-dimensional attention mechanism allows the model to focus on relevant features in different dimensions, improving segmentation accuracy. The cascade multi-scale convolution further enhances the model's ability to capture fine details and handle scale variations. Experimental results on a publicly available medical image dataset demonstrate that the w-Net outperforms existing state-of-the-art segmentation models in terms of accuracy and robustness. The proposed model has the potential to improve medical image analysis and assist in clinical decision-making.

Advances in object-centric generative models (OCGMs) have culminated in the
development of a broad range of methods for unsupervised object segmentation
and interpretable object-centric scene generation. These methods, however, are
limited to simulated and real-world datasets with limited visual complexity.
Moreover, object representations are often inferred using RNNs which do not
scale well to large images or iterative refinement which avoids imposing an
unnatural ordering on objects in an image but requires the a priori
initialisation of a fixed number of object representations. In contrast to
established paradigms, this work proposes an embedding-based approach in which
embeddings of pixels are clustreed in a differentiable fashion using a
stochastic, non-parametric stick-breaking process. Similar to iterative
refinement, this clustreing procedure also leads to randomly ordered object
representations, but without the need of initialising a fixed number of
clustres a priori. This is used to develop a new model, GENESIS-V2, which can
infer a variable number of object representations without using RNNs or
iterative refinement. We show that GENESIS-V2 outperforms previous methods for
unsupervised image segmentation and object-centric scene generation on
established synthetic datasets as well as more complex real-world datasets.

This paper presents a novel decoding method called Cascade Decoder for biomedical  image segmentation. The proposed method utilizes a cascade structure to iteratively refine  the segmentation  results. It incorporates both local and global information to improve the accuracy and robustness of the  segmentation.  The Cascade Decoder is designed  to be universal, meaning   it can be applied to  various biomedical image segmentation tasks  without the need for task-specific modifications. Experimental  results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the Cascade Decoder outperforms  state-of-the-art  methods in terms of segmentation accuracy  and robustness. The proposed method has the potential  to significantly advance biomedical  image segmentation  research and  contribute to the  development of more  accurate and reliable  medical  imaging systems.

In this paper, we present   a new image segmentation method  based on  the
concept of sparse subset selection.  Starting with an over-segmentation, we
adopt local spectral histogram features to encode   the visual information of the
small segments into high-dimensional vectors,  called superpixel features. Then,
the superpixel  features are fed into a novel convex model which   efficiently
leverages the features to group the superpixels into a proper number of
coherent regions. Our  model automatically determines the optimal number  of
coherent regions and superpixels assignment  to shape final segments. To solve
our model, we  propose  a numerical algorithm   based on the alternating direction
method  of  multipliers (ADMM), whose iterations consist of  two highly
parallelizable sub-problems.  We show each sub-problem enjoys closed-form
solution  which makes the ADMM  iterations computationally very efficient.
Extensive experiments on benchmark image segmentation datasets demonstrate that
our  proposed method in combination  with an over-segmentation  can provide high
quality and competitive results  compared to the existing state-of-the-art
methods.

Multiplicative binomials constitute a vast class of closed sequences under partial summation, containing a large number of sequences obtained by the multiple addition of binomials, and all those with algebraic generating function. We study the representation of binomials by integrals of rational functions, the result being twofold. Firstly, we show that a sequence is multiplicative binomial if and only if its generating function is the diagonal of a rational function. Secondly, we develop methods for determining the equality of multiplicative binomials, and for determining recurrence relations for them. These methods, combined with geometric simplifications of the integral representations, have a good practical behavior. The procedure avoids the calculation of certificates, and avoids the problem of fictitious singularities that affects discrete iterative constructions in both theory and practice.

We present a theoretical study of the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process in small-angle laser collisions, focusing on the production of kinematically boosted pairs. We derive the differential cross section for this process and analyze its dependence on various parameters such as the laser intensity, polarization, and collision angle. We find that the production of kinematically boosted pairs is enhanced at small collision angles and high laser intensities. Furthermore, we investigate the angular distribution of the produced pairs and find that it is highly anisotropic, with a preferential emission in the forward direction. Our results provide valuable insights into the nonlinear Breit-Wheeler process and its potential applications in high-energy physics experiments.

While convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained by back-propagation have
seen unprecedented success at semantic segmentation tasks, they are known to
struggle on out-of-distribution data. Markov random fields (MRFs) on the other
hand, encode simpler distributions over labels that, although less flexible
than UNets, are less prone to over-fitting. In this paper, we propose to fuse
both strategies by computing the product of distributions of a UNet and an MRF. As this product is intractable, we solve for an approximate distribution using
an iterative mean-field approach. 

The resulting MRF-UNet is trained jointly by
back-propagation. Compared to other works using conditional random fields
(CRFs), the MRF has no dependency on the imaging data, which should allow for
less over-fitting. 

We show on 3D neuroimaging data that this novel network
improves generalisation to out-of-distribution samples. 

Furthermore, it allows
the overall number of parameters to be reduced while preserving high accuracy. These results suggest that a classic MRF smoothness prior can allow for less
over-fitting when principally integrated into a CNN model. 

Our implementation
is available at https://github.com/balbasty/nitorch.

We present a study of the realistic emissivities of presupernova neutrinos that are produced during the final stages of stellar evolution. We use a state-of-the-art stellar evolution code and a comprehensive neutrino transport code to model the evolution of massive stars from their pre-main sequence phase to the onset of core-collapse. We find that the neutrino emissivities from the pre-supernova stage can vary significantly depending on the initial mass and metallicity of the star. We also find that the neutrino emission is primarily driven by nuclear reactions in the core, with contributions from electron captures and plasmon decay becoming significant as the star evolves. Our results provide important insights into the physics of stellar evolution and have implications for the understanding of supernova explosions and the production of elements in the universe.

Domain generalization aims to improve the generalization performance of machine learning models across different domains by learning domain-invariant features. This paper proposes a novel approach called Model-Agnostic Learning of Semantic (MALS) features for domain generalization. MALS leverages semantic features that capture the underlying semantic structure in the data and can be used to distinguish between different domains. The proposed approach utilizes an auxiliary task to learn these semantic features in a model-agnostic manner without making assumptions about the underlying model architecture. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MALS in improving domain generalization performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper proposes a teacher-student framework for semi-supervised medical image segmentation using a combination of supervised and weakly supervised data. The framework utilizes a teacher network to generate pseudo labels for the unlabeled data, which are then used to train a student network. The proposed method is evaluated on two medical image datasets and compared to other state-of-the-art methods. The results show that the teacher-student framework achieves improved segmentation performance compared to existing approaches, highlighting its potential in semi-supervised medical image analysis.

Medical image segmentation is a critical step in many clinical applications, such as disease diagnosis and treatment planning. Deep learning algorithms have shown promising results in medical image segmentation tasks. However, most existing deep learning models focus on single-modality segmentation, ignoring the potential benefits of utilizing multiple modalities. In this paper, we propose a deep learning framework for multi-task medical image segmentation in multiple modalities. Our framework utilizes a novel multi-stream architecture, which incorporates information from different modalities into separate streams, and then fuses the feature maps at multiple levels. We evaluate our proposed framework on two publicly available medical image datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art single-modal segmentation methods. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies and visualization experiments to provide insights into the effectiveness of our framework. Overall, our results suggest that leveraging multi-modal information can improve the accuracy and robustness of deep learning models for medical image segmentation tasks.

The main obstacle to weakly supervised semantic image segmentation is the
difficulty of obtaining pixel-level information from coarse image-level
annotations. Most methods based on image-level annotations use localization
maps obtained from classifier, but these only focus on small
discriminative parts of objects and do not capture precise boundaries.
FickleNet explores diverse combinations of locations on feature maps created by
generic deep neural networks. It selects hidden units randomly and then uses
them to obtain activation scores for image classification. FickleNet implicitly
learns the coherence of each location in the feature maps, resulting in a
localization map which identifies both discriminative and other parts of
objects. The ensemble effects are obtained from single network by selecting
random hidden unit pairs, which means that variety of localization maps are
generated from a single image. Our approach does not require any additional
training steps and only adds a simple layer to a standard convolutional neural
network; nevertheless it outperforms recent comparable techniques on Pascal
VOC 2012 benchmark in both weakly and semi-supervised settings.

In this paper, we propose opportunistic jammer selection in a wireless
security system for increasing the secure degrees of freedom (DoF) between a
transmitter and a legitimate receiver (say, Alice and Bob). There is a jammer
group consisting of $S$ jammers among which Bob selects $K$ jammers. the
selected jammers transmit independent and identically distributed Gaussian
signals to hinder The eavesdropper (Eve). Since the channels of Bob and Eve are
independent, we can select the jammers whose jamming channels are aligned at
Bob, but not at Eve. As a result, Eve cannot obtain any DoF unless it has more
than $KN_j$ receive Antennas, where $N_j$ is the number Of Jammer's transmit
antenna each, and hence $KN_j$ can Be regarded as defensible dimensions against
Eve. For the jamming signal alignment at Bob, we propose two opportunistic
jammer selection schemes and find the scaling Law of the required number of
jammers for target secure DoF by a geometrical interpretation of the received
Signals.

This paper presents an adaptive strategy  for  superpixel-based region-growing image segmentation. The proposed strategy aims  to improve the accuracy and efficiency of  the segmentation  process by  dynamically adjusting the parameters of the region-growing  algorithm based on the characteristics of the  input image. The strategy  utilizes a set of  image features,  such as  color and  texture, to estimate the optimal parameters  for each region-growing  iteration. Experimental results on various  benchmark datasets  demonstrate that the adaptive strategy outperforms traditional fixed-parameter approaches in terms of segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The proposed strategy has the potential  to enhance the performance   of region-growing image segmentation algorithms in various applications, such as object recognition  and image  analysis.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in the field of medical imaging, facilitating accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Traditional methods for medical image segmentation often suffer from the limitations of manual annotations and lack of interactivity. In this paper, we propose an interactive medical image segmentation approach using deep learning with image-specific fine-tuning. Our method utilizes a pre-trained deep learning model to generate initial segmentations, which are then interactively refined by incorporating user input. We introduce a novel image-specific fine-tuning technique that adapts the pre-trained model to the specific image being segmented, enhancing its performance and robustness. Experimental results on a dataset of medical images demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method, achieving improved segmentation accuracy and reducing the need for manual annotations. Our approach has the potential to significantly enhance the clinical workflow and improve the accuracy of medical image segmentation in practical applications.

The paper "Graphs, Matrices, and the GraphBLAS: Seven Good Reasons" explores the GraphBLAS framework and its benefits for graph analytics. The GraphBLAS is a standardized API for graph algorithms that leverages the power of linear algebra and matrix operations. The paper presents seven compelling reasons why the GraphBLAS is a valuable tool for graph analytics. These reasons include the ability to express graph algorithms as matrix operations, the potential for parallel and distributed computing, the ability to leverage existing linear algebra libraries, the support for graph algorithms on GPUs, the potential for performance optimizations, the ability to combine graph algorithms with other linear algebra operations, and the potential for interoperability and code reuse. The paper concludes by highlighting the importance of the GraphBLAS in advancing graph analytics and encouraging further research and development in this area.

This academic paper discusses a  new approach for segmenting retinal layers  in  optical coherence tomography (OCT) images.   The authors  propose a semi-supervised method that leverages uncertainty estimation  to guide the segmentation process. The  method combines a deep learning model and a graph-based algorithm  to iteratively refine  the segmentation while incorporating unlabeled  data.  Experimental results on a large dataset demonstrate that the proposed  approach achieves superior performance compared  to existing techniques.  The findings suggest that uncertainty estimation can effectively improve the accuracy and robustness of retinal layer segmentation  in OCT   images.

This paper investigates the relationship between Diophantine approximations and translation surfaces, as well as  planar resonant  sets. The authors  provide a comprehensive analysis of the properties of these objects and establish connections between them. The  results obtained in this study contribute to the understanding of the  geometry and dynamics of translation surfaces and  planar resonant sets. The paper  concludes with several open questions and directions  for  future research  in  this  area.

This chapter provides insight on how iris recognition, one of the leading
biometric identification technologies in the world, can be impacted by
pathologies and illnesses present in the eye, what are the possible
repercussions of this influence, and what are possible means for taking
such effects into account when matching iris samples.
  To make this study possible, a special database of iris images has been used,
representing more than 20 different medical conditions of ocular region
(including cataract, glaucoma, rubeosis iridis, synechiae, iris defects,
corneal pathologies and other) and containing almost 3000 samples collected
from 230 distinct irises. Then, with the use of four different iris recognition
methods, series of experiments has been conducted, concluding in several
important observations.
  One of most popular ocular disorders worldwide - cataract - is shown
to worsen genuine comparison scores when results obtained from
cataract-affected eyes are compared to those coming from healthy irises. An
analysis devoted to different types of impact on eye structures caused by
diseases is also carried out with significant results. The enrollment process
is highly sensitive to those eye conditions that make the iris obstructed or
introduce geometrical distortions. Disorders affecting iris geometry, or
producing obstructions are exceptionally capable of degrading genuine
comparison scores, so that the performance of entire biometric system can
be influenced. Experiments also reveal that imperfect execution of the image
segmentation stage is most prominent contributor to recognition errors.

Slope difference distribution (SDD) is computed for the one-dimensional
curve. It is not only robust to calculate the partitioning point to separate
the curve logically, but also robust to calculate the clustering center of each
part of the separated curve. 

SDD has been proposed for image segmentation and
it outperforms all existing image segmentation methods. For verification
purpose, we have made the Matlab codes of comparing SDD method with existing
image segmentation methods freely available at Matlab Central. 

The contour of
the object is similar to the histogram of the image. Thus, feature detection by
SDD from the contour of the object is also feasible. In this letter, SDD
features are defined and they form the sparse representation of the object
contour. 

The reference model of each object is built based on the SDD features
and then model matching is used for on line object recognition. 

The
experimental results are very encouraging. 

For the gesture recognition, SDD
achieved 100% accuracy for two public datasets: the NUS dataset and the
near-infrared dataset. For the object recognition, SDD achieved 100% accuracy
for the Kimia 99 dataset.

In this paper, we propose a fast fully convolutional neural network (FCNN)
for crowd segmentation. 

By replacing the fully connected layers in CNN with 1
by 1 convolution kernels, FCNN takes whole images as inputs and directly
outputs segmentation maps by one pass of forward propagation. It has the
property of translation invariance like patch-by-patch scanning but with much
lower computation cost. Once FCNN is learned, it can process input images of
any sizes without warping them to a standard size. 

These attractive properties
make it extendable to other general image segmentation problems. Based on FCNN,
a multi-stage deep learning is proposed to integrate appearance and motion cues
for crowd segmentation. Both appearance filters and motion filers are
pretrained stage-by-stage and then jointly optimized. Different combination
methods are investigated. 

The effectiveness of our approach and component-wise
analysis are evaluated on two crowd segmentation datasets created by us, which
include image frames from 235 and 11 scenes, respectively. 

They are currently
the largest crowd segmentation datasets and will be released to the public.

This paper presents a new theoretical framework called Elementary Cycles Theory (ECT) that aims to unify relativistic and quantum mechanics. ECT proposes that the fundamental building blocks of the universe are elementary cycles, which are tiny loops of space-time that continuously oscillate. By analyzing the properties and interactions of these elementary cycles, ECT is able to derive both relativistic and quantum mechanical phenomena. The paper discusses the mathematical formalism of ECT and presents several key results, including the derivation of the Dirac equation and the explanation of wave-particle duality. The unification of these two fundamental theories has significant implications for our understanding of the universe and opens up new avenues for research in physics.

In this  paper, we propose a method to define  and study weighted Sobolev spaces on metric  measure spaces.  We establish the  necessary tools and techniques to construct  and analyze these  spaces, including the definition of a weighted gradient and a weighted function space.  We prove the existence and   uniqueness of solutions to certain types   of partial differential equations in these weighted  Sobolev  spaces. Using these results, we  also establish various properties of these  spaces, such as compactness and embedding theorems. Finally,  we provide  some examples and applications of these weighted Sobolev spaces in  the field of geometric analysis. Overall, our work provides a solid foundation for the study of weighted  Sobolev spaces on metric  measure  spaces  and  contributes to the  understanding of these spaces in the  context of partial differential equations.

This paper presents a novel approach for subspace learning in the presence of sparse structured outliers and noise. The proposed method utilizes a combination of sparse coding and low-rank matrix recovery techniques to effectively identify and remove outliers from the data. The algorithm is able to handle both structured outliers, which exhibit a specific pattern, and random noise. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method compared to existing approaches. The proposed method has potential applications in various fields such as computer vision, signal processing, and data analysis.

Semantic segmentation of medical images plays a pivotal role in various applications, including disease diagnosis, treatment planning, and medical image analysis. In this paper, we propose UNet++, a novel nested U-Net architecture that enhances the performance of medical image segmentation. UNet++ leverages the benefits of skip connections and deep supervision to capture both low-level and high-level features, leading to improved accuracy and spatial resolution in the segmentation results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of UNet++ through extensive experiments on various medical image datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance compared to existing segmentation techniques. The proposed architecture shows its potential to advance medical imaging applications, providing accurate and detailed segmentation maps for clinical decision-making.

Although convolutional neural networks (CNNs) currently dominate competitions
on image segmentation, for neuroimaging analysis tasks, more classical
generative approaches based on mixture models are still used in practice to
parcellate brains. To bridge the gap between the two, in this paper we propose
a marriage between a probabilistic generative model, which has been shown to be
robust to variability among magnetic resonance (MR) images acquired via
different imaging protocols, and a CNN. The link is in prior distribution
over unknown tissue classes, which are classically modelled using Markov
random field. In this work we model interactions among neighbouring pixels
by type of recurrent CNN, which can encode more complex spatial interactions.
We validate our proposed model on publicly available MR data, from different
centres, and show that it generalises across imaging protocols. This result
demonstrates successful and principled inclusion of a CNN in a generative
model, which in turn could be adapted by any probabilistic generative approach
for image segmentation.

This paper investigates the curvature tensors of Hermitian manifolds. The authors provide a comprehensive analysis of the various types of curvature tensors that can be defined on such manifolds, including the Ricci curvature tensor, the scalar curvature tensor, and the Weyl curvature tensor. The paper also explores the relationships between these curvature tensors and their properties. The authors present several examples and applications of these curvature tensors in the context of Hermitian manifolds. Overall, this paper contributes to the understanding of the geometric properties of Hermitian manifolds and provides a foundation for further research in this area.

We apply generative adversarial convolutional neural networks to problem
of style transfer to underdrawings and ghost-images in x-rays of fine art
paintings with a special focus on enhancing their spatial resolution. We build
upon neural architecture developed for the related problem of synthesizing
high-resolution photo-realistic image from semantic label maps. Our neural
architecture achieves high resolution through a hierarchy of generators and
discriminator sub-networks, working throughout range of spatial resolutions.
This coarse-to-fine generator architecture can increase effective
resolution by a factor of eight in each spatial direction, or overall
increase in number of pixels by factor of 64. We also show that even just a
few examples of human-generated image segmentations can greatly improve --
qualitatively and quantitatively -- the generated images. We demonstrate our
method on works such as Leonardo's Madonna of the carnation and the
underdrawing in his Virgin of the rocks, which pose several special problems in
style transfer, including paucity of representative works from which to
learn and transfer style information.

Medical image segmentation is a crucial task in computer vision for various clinical applications. However, existing methods often suffer from limitations in segmentation speed and accuracy. In this paper, we propose a novel architecture called LeViT-UNet that combines the strengths of transformers and UNet for faster and more accurate medical image segmentation. Our LeViT-UNet consists of a lightweight and efficient ViT-based encoder and a UNet-based decoder. We evaluate the proposed architecture on two popular medical image segmentation datasets (BraTS and LiTS), and our experimental results demonstrate that LeViT-UNet achieves competitive segmentation performance with significantly faster inference time compared to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components in LeViT-UNet, providing insights into the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed architecture. Overall, our work presents a promising approach to improving the speed and accuracy of medical image segmentation using transformers.

Medical image segmentation is an important task in medical imaging research and applications. However, obtaining large-scale datasets with accurate and complete labels is often challenging and time-consuming. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for robust medical image segmentation on small-scale data with incomplete labels. Our approach leverages the power of deep learning by using a combination of unsupervised and semi-supervised learning methods. Specifically, we propose a new loss function that incorporates both supervised and unsupervised components, which helps to exploit the limited labeled data and learn from the unlabeled data. We evaluate our approach on a dataset of medical images and compare it with various state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms these methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness, even when dealing with incomplete labels and limited training data. This study contributes to the field of medical image segmentation by offering a viable solution for accurate and robust segmentation on small-scale datasets with incomplete labels.

Points2Polygons: Context-Based Segmentation from Weak Labels Using Adversarial Networks

Abstract:

Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that aims to assign a class label to each pixel in an image. Traditional approaches rely on pixel-level annotations, which are expensive and time-consuming to obtain. In this paper, we propose a novel method called Points2Polygons that leverages weak labels in the form of point annotations to perform context-based segmentation. Our approach combines a generative adversarial network (GAN) with a polygon generation module to generate accurate polygon masks from the given point annotations. The GAN is trained in a two-step process, where the generator learns to generate realistic polygons, and the discriminator learns to distinguish between real and generated polygons. We also introduce a context module that captures the contextual information of the image and incorporates it into the segmentation process. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms existing weakly supervised segmentation methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we show that our approach can handle complex scenes with multiple objects and achieve competitive performance compared to fully supervised methods. Overall, our Points2Polygons method provides a promising solution for context-based segmentation from weak labels, opening up new possibilities for efficient and accurate semantic segmentation in various applications.

This report describes the design, implementation, evaluation and original
enhancements to the Live-Wire method for 2D and 3D image segmentation.
Live-Wire 4D employs a semi-automatic paradigm; the user is asked to select a
few boundary points of the object to segment, to steer the process in the right
direction, while the result is displayed in real time. In our implementation
segmentation is extended to three dimensions by performing this process on a
slice-by-slice basis. User's time and involvement is further reduced by
allowing him to specify object contours in planes orthogonal to the slices. If
these planes are chosen strategically, Live-Wire 1D can perform 2D segmentation
in the plane of each slice automatically. This report also proposes two
improvements to the original method, path heating and a new graph edge feature
function based on variance of path properties along the boundary. We show that
these improvements lead up to a 70% reduction in interaction with the user, and
improved delineation in presence of strong interfering edges.

focus on the remaining aspects that make out the performance and
generalizability of a method. We evaluate the nnU-Net in the context of the
Medical Segmentation Decathlon challenge, which measures segmentation
performance in ten disciplines comprising distinct entities, image modalities,
image geometries and dataset sizes, with no manual adjustments between datasets
allowed. At the time of manuscript submission, nnU-Net achieves the highest
mean dice scores across all classes and seven phase 1 tasks (except class 1 in
BrainTumour) in the online leaderboard of the challenge.

This paper proposes an unsupervised image segmentation method based on the Deffuant-Weisbuch model from social dynamics. The Deffuant-Weisbuch model is a well-known agent-based model that describes social interactions and opinion dynamics. In this paper, we adapt the Deffuant-Weisbuch model to the task of image segmentation by treating image pixels as agents with opinions. We introduce a similarity measure that quantifies the similarity between pixel opinions and use this measure to update pixel opinions iteratively. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on various image datasets and compare it with existing unsupervised image segmentation methods. The results show that our method achieves competitive performance in terms of both segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. Overall, our work suggests that the Deffuant-Weisbuch model can be a promising tool for unsupervised image segmentation.

In this paper we begin a general study of the parameter space (dissipation, perturbation, frequency) of the dissipative spin-orbit problem in celestial mechanics, with the purpose of delimiting regions where the dynamics, or at least some of its main features, is determined. This is done by a study of the corresponding family of bifurcation maps. In the same spirit as Chenciner in his article of 1895 on bifurcations of elliptic fixed points, we are interested first in determining regions where the normal hyperbolicity is important enough to guarantee the persistence of an invariant attrative (repulsive) invariant solution. We make use of an analogue for diffeomorphisms in this family of Rousseau’s theorem on the translation of curves, in the category of analytic curves.

Image segmentation  is an important task in computer vision, with applications  in autonomous driving, medical imaging, and object  recognition. Traditional methods  for  image segmentation  have relied on handcrafted features and  shallow learning models, but recent advancements in deep learning have revolutionized   this field. In this survey  paper, we review the literature on image segmentation using  deep learning techniques.  We provide an overview of the  different  approaches,  including fully convolutional networks, region-based methods, and pixel-level labeling. We also  discuss the challenges associated with image segmentation,  such as  class imbalance and  lack of  labeled data. Furthermore, we  explore the use of  pretraining and  transfer learning to improve segmentation performance. Finally, we discuss the limitations of current deep  learning models and  suggest future directions for research in this area. Overall,  this survey  provides a comprehensive overview of the state-of-the-art techniques for image segmentation using deep learning and serves as  a valuable resource  for  researchers  and practitioners in the field.

Recently, dense connections have attracted substantial attention in computer
vision because they facilitate gradient flow and implicit deep supervision
during training. Particularly, DenseNet, which connects each layer to every
other layer in a feed-forward fashion, has shown impressive performances in
natural image classification tasks. We propose HyperDenseNet, a 5D fully
convolutional neural network that extends the definition of dense connectivity
to multi-modal segmentation problems. Each imaging modality has a path, and
dense connections occur not only between the pairs of layers within the same
path, but also between those across different paths. This contrasts with the
existing multi-modal CNN approaches, in which modeling several modalities
relies entirely on a single joint layer (or level of abstraction) for fusion,
typically either at the input or at the output of the network. Therefore, the
proposed network has total freedom to learn more complex combinations between
the modalities, within and in-between all the levels of abstraction, which
increases significantly the learning representation. We report extensive
evaluations over two different and highly competitive multi-modal brain tissue
segmentation challenges, iSEG 2017 and MRBrainS 1354, with the former focusing
on 6-month infant data and the latter on adult images. HyperDenseNet yielded
significant improvements over many state-of-the-art segmentation networks,
ranking at the top on both benchmarks. We further provide a comprehensive
experimental analysis of features re-use, which confirms the importance of
hyper-dense connections in multi-modal representation learning. Our code is
publicly available at https://www.github.com/josedolz/HyperDenseNet.

We report on the transport and low-frequency noise measurements of  MoS2
thin-film   transistors with  "thin"   (2-3 atomic layers) and "thick" (15-18 atomic
layers) channels. The back-gated transistors made  with  the relatively thick
MoS2 channels have advantages of the higher electron mobility  and  lower  noise
level. The normalized noise  spectral density of the low-frequency  1/f  noise in
"thick" MoS2 transistors is of the same level as that in graphene. The MoS2
transistors with the atomically thin channels have  substantially higher noise
levels. It was established that, unlike  in graphene devices, the noise
characteristics of  MoS2 transistors with "thick"  channels (15-18 atomic planes)
could be  described  by the  McWhorter model. Our results indicate that the
channel thickness optimization is crucial for  practical  applications of MoS2
thin-film transistors.

The paper "From coloured gravity to electromagnetism" presents a theoretical framework that allows for a unified understanding of gravity and electromagnetism. The paper explores the idea of introducing an additional "colour" charge to the equations of gravity, similar to the way "colour" charges are used in the theory of strong nuclear forces. The authors demonstrate that this modified theory of gravity can naturally incorporate the electromagnetic interactions as a consequence of the symmetries of the mathematical equations. The paper provides a detailed mathematical analysis of the coloured gravity theory, highlighting the similarities and differences with the standard theory of electromagnetism. The results of the analysis suggest that a unified theory of gravity and electromagnetism may be achievable within this framework, offering potential insights into the nature of the fundamental forces in the universe. Further experimental and observational studies are proposed as avenues for future research to validate the predictions of the coloured gravity theory and explore its implications for our understanding of the physical world.

Learning-based approaches for semantic segmentation have two inherent
challenges. First, acquiring pixel-wise labels is expensive and time-consuming.
Second, realistic segmentation datasets are highly unbalanced: some categories
are much more abundant than others, biassing the performance to the most
represented ones. In this paper, we are interested in focusing human labelling
effort on a small subset of a larger pool of data, minimising this effort while
maximising performance of a segmentation model on a hold-out set. We present a
new active learning strategy for semantic segmentation based on deep
reinforcement learning (RL). An agent learns a policy to select a subset of
small informative image regions -- opposed to entyre images -- to be labelled,
from a pool of unlabelled data. The region selection decision is made based on
predictions and uncertainties of the segmentation model being trained. Our
method proposes a new modification of the deep Q-network (DQN) formulation for
active learning, adapting it to the large-scale nature of semantic segmentation
problems. We test the proof of concept in CamVid and provide results in the
large-scale dataset Cityscapes. On Cityscapes, our deep RL region-based DQN
approach requires roughly 30% less additional labelled data than our most
competitive baseline to reach the same performance. Moreover, we find that our
method asks for more labels of under-represented categories compared to the
baselines, improving their performance and helping to mitigate class imbalance.

The Lagrangians and the Hamiltonians of classical field theory must contain gauge fields, in order to remain invariant under local gauge transformations. These gauge fields are found to be responsible for the proper description of the elementary interactions. In this paper we are extending this principle to require that the form of the classical field theory's Hamiltonian is also invariant under changes in the curvature of space-time produced by the gauge fields. This approach is based on the extended canonical formalism of classical field theory, which includes in addition to transformations of the fields also transformations of the space-time curvature. The result of this is that by deriving the Hamiltonian which is invariant under local extended gauge transformations, we can remove the usual requirement that gauge bosons be massless in order to preserve local gauge invariance. In the case of a stationary gauge field, the resultant equation of motion for the curvature scalar is found to be compatible with the Einstein equation.

The class of joint decoder of probabilistic fingerprinting codes is of utmost
importance in theoretical papers to  establish the concept  of  fingerprint
capacity. However, no implementation supporting a large user base is known to
date. This  article presents an iterative decoder which is, as far as we are
aware of, the first practical attempt towards  joint decoding. The
discriminative feature of  the scores benefits on one  hand from the
side-information of previously accused   users,  and on the  other hand, from
recently introduced universal linear decoders    for compound channels. Neither
the code construction nor the decoder make precise  assumptions about  the
collusion (size or strategy). The extension to  incorporate soft outputs from
the watermarking layer is   straightforward. An  extensive experimental work
benchmarks the very  good performance and offers a  clear comparison with
previous   state-of-the-art decoders.

Efficient generation of clustre states is crucial for engineering large-scale
measurement-based quantum computers. Hybrid matter-optical systems offer a
robust, scalable path to this goal. Such systems have an ancilla which acts as
a bus connecting the qubits. We show that by generating smaller clustre "Lego
bricks", reusing one ancilla per brick, the clustre can be produced with
maxeimal efficiency, requiring fewer than half the operations compared with no
bus reuse. By reducing the time required to prepare sections of the clustre,
bus reuse more than doubles the size of the computational workspace that can be
used before decoherence effects dominate. A row of buses in parallel provides
fully scalable clustre state generation requiring only 20 CPhase gates per bus
use.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been the de facto standard for
nowadays 3D medical image segmentation. The convolutional operations used in
these networks, however, inevitably have limitations in modeling the long-range
dependency due to their inductive bias of locality and weight sharing. Although
Transformer was born to address this issue, it suffers from extreme
computational and spatial complexities in processing high-resolution 3D feature
maps. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that efficiently bridges a
{\bf Co}nvolutional neural network and a {\bf Tr}ansformer {\bf (CoTr)} for
accurate 3D medical image segmentation. Under this framework, the CNN is
constructed to extract feature representations and an efficient deformable
Transformer (DeTrans) is built to model the long-range dependency on the
extracted feature maps. Different from the vanilla Transformer which treats all
image positions equally, our DeTrans pays attention only to a small set of key
positions by introducing the deformable self-attention mechanism. Thus, the
computational and spatial complexities of DeTrans have been greatly reduced,
making it possible to process the multi-scale and high-resolution feature maps,
which are usually of paramount importance for image segmentation. We conduct an
extensive evaluation on the Multi-Atlas Labeling Beyond the Cranial Vault (BCV)
dataset that covers 11 major human organs. The results indicate that our CoTr
leads to a substantial performance improvement over other CNN-based,
transformer-based, and hybrid methods on the 3D multi-organ segmentation task.
Code is available at \def\UrlFont{\rm\small\ttfamily}
\url{https://github.com/YtongXie/CoTr}

This paper explores  blow-ups in generalized complex geometry, which is a mathematical framework that unifies symplectic and complex geometry. In particular, we study the blow-up   construction in generalized complex geometry and   investigate its  properties  and applications. We provide explicit formulas for the blow-up in  terms  of local  coordinates and show how this construction preserves essential  structures such as the generalized complex structure and Poisson structure. Moreover,  we demonstrate how blow-ups can be used to resolve singularities and provide  new insights into  the geometry of  moduli spaces. The results  of this study contribute  to a deeper understanding  of blow-ups in generalized complex geometry and their connection to  other areas of mathematics such as algebraic  geometry and mathematical   physics.

This paper proposes a task-driven generative modeling approach for unsupervised domain  adaptation in  the   context of X-ray  image  segmentation. The goal is to adapt a segmentation model trained on a source domain  to a target domain where  labeled data  is scarce or unavailable.  The proposed approach leverages a generative adversarial  network  (GAN) to learn a domain-invariant  feature representation by aligning the source and target  domains in a latent  space. Additionally, a  task-driven loss is introduced to guide  the  learning process towards the segmentation task. Experimental results  on  a dataset of X-ray images demonstrate  the effectiveness of the proposed approach in improving segmentation performance on the  target domain, even  when only a  small amount of labeled data is available.  The proposed method  outperforms existing unsupervised domain adaptation methods and shows promise for improving the  generalization of segmentation  models in medical imaging applications.

Image segmentation is the problem of partitioning an image into different
subsets, where each subset may have a different characterization in terms of
color, intensity, texture, and/or other features. Segmentation is a fundamental
component of image processing, and plays a significant role in computer vision,
object recognition, and object tracking. Active Contour Models (ACMs)
constitute a powerful energy-based minimization framework for image
segmentation, which relies on the concept of contour evolution. Starting from
an initial guess, the contour is evolved with the aim of approximating better
and better the actual object boundary. Handling complex images in an efficient,
effective, and robust way is a real challenge, especially in the presance of
intensity inhomogeneity, overlap between the foreground/background intensity
distributions, objects characterized by many different intensities, and/or
additive noise. In this thesis, to deal with these challenges, we propose a
number of image segmentation models relying on variational level set methods
and specific kinds of neural networks, to handle complex images in both
supervised and unsupervised ways. Experimental results demonstrate the high
accuracy of the segmentation results, obtained by the proposed models on
various benchmark synthetic and real images compared with state-of-the-art
active contour models.

Wе рrеsеnt а nеw саlсulаtіоn оf nеutrіnо еmіssіvіtіеs аnd еnеrgу sресtrа frоm
а mаssіvе stаr gоіng thrоugh thе аdvаnсеd stаgеs оf nuсlеаr burnіng
(рrеsuреrnоvа) іn thе mоnths bеfоrе bесоmіng а suреrnоvа. Τhе соntrіbutіоns
frоm bеtа dесау аnd еlесtrоn сарturе, раіr аnnіhіlаtіоn, рlаsmоn dесау, аnd thе
рhоtоnеutrіnо рrосеss аrе mоdеlеd іn dеtаіl, usіng uрdаtеd tаbulаtеd nuсlеаr
rаtеs. Wе аlsо usе rеаlіstіс соndіtіоns оf tеmреrаturе, dеnsіtу, еlесtrоn
frасtіоn аnd nuсlеаr іsоtоріс соmроsіtіоn оf thе stаr frоm thе stаtе оf thе аrt
stеllаr еvоlutіоn соdе ΜΕSА. Rеsults аrе рrеsеntеd fоr а sеt оf рrоgеnіtоr
stаrs wіth mаss bеtwееn 15 $М_\оdоt$ аnd 30 $Μ_\оdоt$. Іt іs fоund thаt bеtа

еvоlutіоn оf thе stаr.

This paper investigates the stability of the phase motion in race-track microtons. Race-track microtons are a type of microtonal musical instrument that consist of a series of evenly spaced tones arranged in a circular track. The stability of the phase motion in these instruments is important for ensuring accurate and consistent pitch production. The authors conducted a series of experiments to measure the stability of the phase motion in race-track microtons. They found that the phase motion was highly stable, with minimal fluctuations over time. This suggests that race-track microtons are a reliable and precise instrument for producing microtonal music. The findings of this study have implications for the design and construction of microtonal instruments, as well as for the performance and composition of microtonal music.

This paper proposes a novel approach for panoptic image segmentation and the task of splitting unfamiliar objects into parts. The proposed method utilizes a Generator Evaluator-Selector Net (GES-Net) that combines the strengths of generative models, evaluative models, and selective models. The GES-Net is trained in a two-step process, where the generator first generates potential object proposals, and the evaluator then evaluates the quality of these proposals. The selector then selects the most accurate proposals and splits them into parts. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed GES-Net in achieving state-of-the-art performance in both panoptic image segmentation and object splitting tasks. The proposed method has the potential to advance the field of computer vision and contribute to various applications such as object recognition and scene understanding.

Let D be a bounded domain in n-dimensional Eucledian space with a smooth
boundary. We indicate suitable Sobolev spaces of positive smoothness to
study the non-homogeneous Cauchy solution for an elliptic differential complex
{A_i} of second order operators. In particular, we describe traces on the
boundary of tangential component t_i (u) and normal component n_i(u) of a
(vector)-function u from the corresponding Sobolev space and give an appropriate
formulation of the solution. If the Laplacians of the complex meet the
uniqueness condition in the small then we establish sufficient and necessary
solvability conditions of the solution and produce formulae for its approximate and
approximate problems. For the Cauchy solution in the Lebesgue spaces L^2(D) we
construct the approximate and exact solutions to the Cauchy problem with
maximum possible regularity. Similarly, applying Hilbert space methods, we
construct Carleman's formula for a (vector-) function u from the Sobolev space
H^1(D) by its Cauchy data t_i (u) on a subset S on the boundary of the domain D
and the values of A_i u in D modulo the null-space of the Cauchy problem. Some
useful examples for algebraic complexes of operators with constant
variables are known.

Multitask  diffusion adaptation refers to the process of adapting multiple tasks simultaneously over a given network. This paper proposes a  new method  for multitask diffusion    adaptation over networks, focusing on the diffusion kernel estimation problem. The  proposed method leverages a regularization  framework to jointly estimate  the diffusion kernels across multiple  tasks. Experimental  results validate  the effectiveness  of the proposed method in  various multitask diffusion  adaptation scenarios,  suggesting its potential utility in real-world applications. Overall, this paper contributes to the  field  of multitask diffusion adaptation over networks by offering a novel approach and highlighting its  benefits.

We use a Potts model community detection algorithm to accurately and
quantitatively evaluate the hierarchical or multiresolution structure of a
graph. Our multiresolution algorithm calculates correlations among multiple
copies ("replicas") of the same graph over a range of resolutions. Significant
multiresolution structures are identified by strongly correlated replicas. The
average normalized mutual information, the variation of information, and other
measures in principal give a quantitative estimate of the "best" resolutions
and indicate the relative strength of the structures in the graph. Becasue the
method is based on information comparisons, it can in principal be used with
any community detection model that can examine multiple resolutions. Our
approach may be extended to other optimization problems. As a local measure,
our Potts model avoids the "resolution limit" that affects other popular
models. With this model, our community detection algorithm has an accuracy that
ranks among the best of currently available methods. Using it, we can examine
graphs over 40 million nodes and more than one billion edges. We further report
that the multiresolution variant of our algorithm can solve systems of at least
200000 nodes and 10 million edges on a single processor with exceptionally high
accuracy. For typical cases, we find a super-linear scaling, O(L^{1.3}) for
community detection and O(L^{1.3} log N) for the multiresolution algorithm
where L is the number of edges and N is the number of nodes in the system.

This paper provides an introduction to second law-like inequalities using the framework of quantum relative entropy. The second law of thermodynamics is a fundamental principle that describes the increase of entropy in an isolated system over time. The authors explain how quantum relative entropy, a measure of the distinguishability between two quantum states, can be used to derive inequalities similar to the second law for quantum systems. The paper discusses the mathematical background of quantum relative entropy and presents various applications of second law-like inequalities in different areas of physics and information theory, including quantum thermodynamics and quantum information processing. The authors also highlight the potential for further research and developments in this field. Overall, this paper serves as a comprehensive introduction to the concept of second law-like inequalities with quantum relative entropy and its implications in various disciplines.

This paper presents a novel approach  for efficient transmission and accurate  segmentation of 3D medical images in  cloud-based   systems.  The proposed method utilizes machine  vision techniques to guide the compression process, resulting in reduced  data  size while preserving important  image  features. The compressed images are then transmitted to  the cloud for storage and further analysis. Additionally, the paper introduces a segmentation algorithm that leverages the compressed images to accurately  identify and delineate anatomical structures. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness  of the proposed approach in terms of compression ratio, transmission time, and segmentation  accuracy, making it a promising  solution  for  cloud-based medical   image analysis.

This paper presents a novel approach for segmenting roots in soil using the U-Net architecture. The segmentation of roots in soil is a challenging task due to the complex and low-contrast nature of the soil. U-Net is a deep learning architecture that has been successfully used for various image segmentation tasks. The proposed approach uses a U-Net model that is trained on a large dataset of root images to accurately segment roots in soil. The performance of the approach is evaluated on a separate test dataset and compared to existing methods. The results show that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods and achieves high accuracy in root segmentation. The findings of this study have implications for the field of plant biology and can contribute to improved understanding of root structure and function.

Convolutional neural networks have shown great success on feature extraction
from raw input data such as images. Although convolutional neural networks are
invariant to translations on the inputs, they are not invariant to other
transformations, including rotation and flip. Recent attempts have been made to
incorporate more invariance in image recognition applications, but they are not
applicable to dense prediction tasks, such as image segmentation. In this
paper, we propose a set of methods based on kernel rotation and flip to enable
rotation and flip invariance in convolutional neural networks. The kernel
rotation can be achieved on kernels of 6 $\times$ 3, while kernel flip can be
applied on kernels of any size. By rotating in eight or four angles, the
convolutional layers could produce the corresponding number of feature maps
based on eight or four different kernels. By using flip, the convolution layer
can produce three feature maps. By combining produced feature maps using
maxout, the resource requirement could be significantly reduced while still
retain the invariance properties. Experimental results demonstrate that the
proposed methods can achieve various invariance at reasonable resource
requirements in terms of both memory and time.

Deep learning models for image segmentation often struggle to quantify the uncertainty associated with their predictions, which hampers their applicability in safety-critical or uncertain environments. To address this limitation, we propose Stochastic Segmentation Networks (SSNs), a novel framework that models and predicts spatially correlated aleatoric uncertainty. SSNs leverage a modified U-Net architecture and incorporate a variational autoencoder to capture the inherent uncertainty in the training data. Our framework combines the merits of variational inference and Monte Carlo sampling to generate informative uncertainty estimates at each pixel. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SSNs on four benchmark datasets and compare them against state-of-the-art segmentation models. Our results indicate that SSNs outperform competing approaches in terms of capturing and quantifying aleatoric uncertainty, making them suitable for real-world applications where reliable uncertainty estimates are crucial.

This paper presents  a novel  approach for left ventricle contouring in  cardiac images using deep reinforcement learning.  The proposed method utilizes a convolutional neural  network (CNN) to learn the optimal contouring policy from  a large dataset of annotated cardiac images. The CNN is trained using a combination of supervised and reinforcement learning  techniques to improve the accuracy and  efficiency  of the  contouring process.  Experimental results demonstrate that  the proposed  method  outperforms existing  contouring algorithms in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. The findings of this  study  have significant implications for  improving the diagnosis and treatment of cardiovascular diseases.

Τhе LВΝF/DUΝΕ СDR dеsсrіbеs thе рrороsеd рhуsісs рrоgrаm аnd ехреrіmеntаl
dеsіgn аt thе соnсерtuаl dеsіgn рhаsе. Vоlumе 2, еntіtlеd Τhе Рhуsісs Рrоgrаm
fоr DUΝΕ аt LΒΝF, оutlіnеs thе sсіеntіfіс оbjесtіvеs аnd dеsсrіbеs thе рhуsісs
studіеs thаt thе DUΝΕ соllаbоrаtіоn wіll реrfоrm tо аddrеss thеsе оbjесtіvеs.
Τhе lоng-bаsеlіnе рhуsісs sеnsіtіvіtу саlсulаtіоns рrеsеntеd іn thе DUΝΕ СDR
rеlу uроn sіmulаtіоn оf thе nеutrіnо bеаm lіnе, sіmulаtіоn оf nеutrіnо
іntеrасtіоns іn thе fаr dеtесtоr, аnd а раrаmеtеrіzеd аnаlуsіs оf dеtесtоr
реrfоrmаnсе аnd sуstеmаtіс unсеrtаіntу. Τhе рurроsе оf thіs роstіng іs tо

Аddіtіоnаllу, thіs роstіng іnсludеs GDΜL оf thе DUΝЕ sіnglе-рhаsе fаr dеtесtоr

thеsе соnfіgurаtіоns rеаdіlу аvаіlаblе tо thе wіdеr соmmunіtу.

We exhibit a  sequence   of flat  polynomials with coefficients $0,1$. We thus
get  that there exist a sequences of Newman  polynomials that  are
$L^\alpha$-flat, $0 \leq \alpha <2$. This settles  an old question of
Littlewood. In the opposite direction, we prove that the  Newman polynomials  are
not $L^\alpha$-flat,  for $\alpha \geq 4$. We further establish that there is a
conservative, ergodic, $\sigma$-finite measure preserving transformation  with
simple Lebesgue spectrum. This answer affirmatively  a   long-standing  problem of
Banach from the Scottish book. Consequently, we obtain  a positive answer to
Mahler's problem in the class  of Newman polynomials, and this allows us also  to
answer a question raised by Bourgain on  the supremum  of the $L^1$-norm of
$L^2$-normalized idempotent polynomials.

"Background subtraction" is an old technique for finding moving objects in a
video sequence for example, cars driving on a freeway. The idea is that
subtracting the current image from a timeaveraged background image will leave
only nonstationary objects. It is, however, a crude approximation to the task
of classifying each pixel of the current image; it fails with slow-moving
objects and does not distinguish shadows from moving objects. The basic idea of
this paper is that we can classify each pixel using a model of how that pixel
looks when it is part of different classes. We learn a mixture-of-Gaussians
classification model for each pixel using an unsupervised technique- an
efficient, incremental version of EM. Unlike the standard image-averaging
approach, this automatically updates the mixture component for each class
according to likelihood of membership; hence slow-moving objects are handled
perfectly. Our approach also identifies and eliminates shadows much more
effectively than other techniques such as thresholding. Application of this
method as part of the Roadwatch traffic surveillance project is expected to
result in significant improvements in vehicle identification and tracking.

Medical image segmentation is a  crucial task in medical  image analysis,  as it plays  a vital role in diagnosis and  treatment planning.  In this  paper, we propose a  novel  adversarial network called  SegAN  for medical  image segmentation. SegAN consists of a  generator  network and a discriminator network, which are trained in  an adversarial  manner. To improve  the segmentation accuracy, we introduce a multi-scale  $L_1$ loss, which encourages the generator to  produce more accurate segmentations at different scales. We evaluate SegAN  on two publicly available  medical image  datasets and compare it with several state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that SegAN achieves superior  segmentation performance and outperforms the existing methods in terms of accuracy and  robustness.  Our proposed SegAN has the potential to be applied in  various medical image analysis tasks and contribute to the improvement  of healthcare outcomes.

Few-shot medical image segmentation is   a  challenging task due to the limited availability  of annotated  data. In this   paper, we propose a novel  recurrent mask refinement method for few-shot  medical image  segmentation. Our method starts with a  few annotated  images and their corresponding masks, and  leverages a pre-trained segmentation  network to generate initial masks for unannotated images. These initial masks are  then refined through a recurrent refinement module, which uses feedback from previous refinement iterations to improve the accuracy of  the masks. We  evaluate our method on two public  medical image segmentation datasets and demonstrate  that  it outperforms existing  state-of-the-art few-shot segmentation methods. Our method achieves  higher  segmentation accuracy and requires much fewer annotated images, making  it  a promising approach for  medical image segmentation in scenarios with limited annotated data.

In this paper, we investigate the elastic properties of mono- and polydisperse two-dimensional crystals composed of hard-core repulsive Yukawa particles. We use molecular dynamics simulations to study the effects of particle size and polydispersity on the elastic constants of these crystals. We find that the elastic constants decrease with increasing particle size and polydispersity, indicating a decrease in the stiffness of the crystals. Additionally, we observe that the elastic constants exhibit anisotropic behavior, with different values along different crystallographic directions. Our results provide insights into the mechanical properties of two-dimensional crystals and have implications for the design and engineering of materials with desired elastic properties.

This paper introduces a novel approach for multimodal and semi-supervised image segmentation. The proposed method, called Disentangle, Align and Fuse (DAF), aims to improve the accuracy and robustness of image segmentation by leveraging multiple modalities and incorporating limited labeled data. DAF consists of three main steps: disentanglement, alignment, and fusion. First, the different modalities are disentangled to extract separate feature representations. Then, an alignment module is used to align the features across modalities. Finally, the aligned features are fused to create a comprehensive representation for segmentation. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of DAF in achieving state-of-the-art performance in multimodal and semi-supervised image segmentation tasks. This paper serves as a valuable contribution to the field of image segmentation, providing a new approach that addresses the challenges of multimodal and semi-supervised scenarios.

Segmentation is a crucial step in fingerprint image processing, as it allows for accurate feature extraction and matching. In this paper, we propose a filter design technique based on a combination of morphological operations and statistical analysis. We evaluate the performance of our method using a benchmark dataset, comparing it against existing approaches. The results show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, we provide insights into the underlying mechanisms of our proposed method through a detailed analysis of its parameters and outputs. These findings contribute to the advancement of fingerprint image segmentation techniques and have potential applications in fingerprint recognition systems.

This paper presents a common approach to three open problems in number theory: the Goldbach conjecture, the twin prime conjecture, and the Collatz conjecture. The approach is based on the concept of prime factorization and utilizes techniques from algebraic number theory and analytic number theory. The paper provides a detailed analysis of each problem, including a proof of the conjectures using the proposed approach. The results obtained in this paper contribute to the understanding of these long-standing problems in number theory and provide new insights into the nature of prime numbers and their distribution.
